utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I was told that there are some matters for you to raise, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency. You tell me when I'm supposed -- may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are a few matters to deal with. One of the most important ones is an intention - I hope it's not a decision yet - to work four days a week. We can barely take three days a week, with the resources that we have. Lord Bonomy had actually mentioned that it would be two days per week, involving a team of eight people. The number of my associates has been reduced to five now. One of them is for legal matters, and all the rest cannot really keep up with the workload. In actual fact, I said at the very outset that I would challenge everything but the climate. That is my right, and that is my duty, to challenge everything that is being mis-characterised here and mis-portrayed, all the wrong allegations contained in the indictment, and we believe that that is of great importance for the future of our people -- our peoples, rather, and their reconciliation. Therefore, it is my duty to present at this trial, and it is for you to provide a fair trial to me, to challenge each and every fact that should be challenged. If it's three days, we have a lot of difficulties involved, especially if we were not to get three more associates from the Registry, at least as many as we had so far; that is, a total of eight. However, since all changes, on the basis of which my situation, as a whole, is being curtailed, it is even direct examinations by the OTP that are being shortened. However, that does not diminish in any way the burden of the Defence, even when it's 92 ter, regardless of whether their direct examination is half an hour or an hour and a half. It doesn't make things anything easier for us or it doesn't shorten the proceedings, as far as we're concerned. So the number of facts that we have to deal with, the number of facts that they are going to introduce through a particular witness, remains the same, irrespective of the way they are examining the witness. From the point of view of the Defence, this is an opportunity to conduct exemplary hearings at an exemplary trial that will serve the purposes of international justice. If that is not the case, we are going to be facing difficulties. We are not going to have a fair trial, we are not going to have an opportunity to present everything that we wish to present and everything that we are supposed to do, in view of everything that the Prosecution is accusing us of. So that is our basic objection, and we had hoped in June we would be sitting two days a week only. If the Trial Chamber were to change its decision, and if they were to require that all witnesses testify viva voce rather than 92 -- on the basis of 92 ter, then with eight people we would manage to do something. However, this way, the rhythm is deadly, as far as we are concerned. Resources, time, human capabilities, as it were, all of that is threatening these proceedings. You have noticed that the OTP have new Prosecutors for each and every witness, and we are who we are. It's the five of us, and no one else, so there is no way we can speak of an equality of arms. Their human and financial resources cannot be compared to ours. Therefore, I would like to ask you to look into that possibility, sitting two days a week rather than four, or to have witnesses testify viva voce so that we have more time to challenge everything that can be challenged and disputed. The other matter I wished to raise was the following. Through the kindness of Mr. van Lynden and Mr. Doyle, who were kind enough to meet with the Defence, I found out that they had some kind of notes and some kind of diaries. However, we have had no insight of this nature. You will see during the proceedings that some things have cropped up for the very first time, things that were not contained either in official reports or in TV reports, but they do appear in witness statements or in witness testimony. So the source of these new allegations that work to our detriment have to -- has to be disclosed. If it's not in a TV report, then it's contained in a note-book. That's why we kindly ask to be given the opportunity to have the Victims and Witnesses Unit ask Mr. van Lynden to submit his note-books and diaries, of course, the part that does not have to do with his family and other private affairs. Also from Mr. Doyle, we would like to ask that we have a look at the notes that he had. He had them on the table when we were sitting there and talking, of course. He said that there were a great many private matters contained in these note-books, and we will respect that. If we get these documents from them, even without a subpoena from you, we are going to need some time to study these notes and perhaps even to investigate the matters involved to see whether that is actually the way things took place. So in that case, at least parts of the cross-examination would have to be postponed, because the Defence cannot deal with all of this new material so quickly. We found out about it only yesterday and the day before yesterday. So these are the basic concerns of the Defence at this point in time. We don't know which one is our most important concern; perhaps the first one that I referred to, the question of the rhythm and the time for cross-examination. For example, Mr. van Lynden said that he would have to leave after the first session on Friday. Indeed, that is a very short period of time, and this is a big witness. His reporting affected the world public opinion. He was an eye-witness. He saw both sides. Now, if we were to have this kind of constraint imposed upon us, that would be extremely difficult. If the Trial Chamber so decides, we would be prepared to work all day tomorrow or to have Mr. van Lynden appear some other day when he can; next Monday, or next week, whenever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger or Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me address one of the matters and perhaps touch on one of the others. Mr. Nicholls was present, I gather, at the time of the discussion that the accused referred to and may be better placed to refer to respond to any issues related to the diaries. With respect to the scheduling issue, for the most part, the Prosecution, of course, leaves that matter, which is within the purview of the Court, in the Court's hands, with the following quick observations. First, I cannot recall any specific reference by Judge Bonomy to a two-day-a-week schedule, and, indeed, if there was a reference to two days, I suspect it was not in reference to this particular context, but I didn't want my silence on that issue to be taken as an affirmation that the Prosecution, too, was aware of that particular reference. Secondly, perhaps it goes without saying, but I should note that the accused's perception of his duty to the Serbian people or the Muslim people is not an appropriate guide-line to the issues that are actually involved and the matters that are actually at issue in this case, and it may also signal some of the reasons underpinning disparities between the assessment of what sufficient time for cross-examination consists of between the Defence and the Prosecution or the Court. And, finally, I would simply note that there have been examples of the needless or pointless or even counter-productive expenditure of resources by the Defence on issues that didn't need to be addressed. One came up in a motion recently. That could serve as at least a partial answer to the resource and time issues raised by the accused. And, finally, with respect to the issue of the notes or journals of the witnesses, I just want to make it clear, before any response that Mr. Nicholls has, that this is not a matter of documents in possession of the Prosecution that weren't disclosed. That's not the issue. Apparently, the accused, during the course of his own investigation, has confirmed the existence of these things and now is interested in them. If they arise belatedly, it's for that reason, and that reason only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Do you have anything to add, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Just to confirm, I was going to rise at the beginning today and explain that, unfortunately, Mr. van Lynden has commitments and would need to go back Friday at about 11.00 a.m. for a flight. I informed my friends of that yesterday. We will have the next witness ready at that time. And that -- confirm what Mr. Tieger said about the note-books. We heard about them yesterday during the interview, and there was a request to me at that time from Mr. Karadzic's associates for the note-books, and I explained I don't have them, I haven't seen them, and I'm not sure what the attitude of the witness will be or where they are. So that's something that we'll need to look into, and the Prosecution will assist in any way it can with these note-books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I, before you make a decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond to what Mr. Tieger said just now? First of all, the Prosecution has such a huge advantage. They are counting on a vast amount of 92 bis evidence with people that I'm not even going to see. Among them, there are some witnesses that were never cross-examined or even seen by any Defence team. Also, there is an abundance of statements, written material, and so on. All of that is cropping up, and I have to be given an opportunity to challenge that, or let the Prosecutors say what they're going to give up on. Let them -- let them tell us what is not going to be used as a basis for a sentence. Whatever may lead to a sentence, I need to challenge. I need to cross-examine witnesses, I need to put our case to the witness, everything that we know, and so on. What Mr. Tieger said, that there were questions that should not have been put, that probably relates to legal issues rather than factual issues. If the Prosecution had only three documents against me, all of this would not be required. They have nothing, so now they want me simply to be snowed under, and I think they even need all the dead witnesses that they have to keep in the case file in order to be sure that I'm found guilty. As for Muslims and Serbs, that is an additional matter. Of course, I'm defending myself here, but it is a fact that the importance of this trial goes beyond the importance of a single individual. Enormous illusions have been created. Many took part in the creation of these illusions; the Prosecution, journalists, diplomats, military factors, intelligence services. They created such conditions that things are always boiling in the Balkans and there's always bad blood there. Of course, I'm defending myself, but I want to clarify all of this, not only because I am being charged in this way and can be sentenced therefor, but also because this is of enormous importance for the people living there. I really think the Prosecutors should be more modest when they challenge the capacities of the Defence, because they have such a vast advantage and they have far more resources. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you'll be surprised to hear that the Chamber is minded to sit five days a week from after the recess. In any event, the Chamber will consider the matter, will give a ruling on that matter. Speaking for myself, one potential solution may be to have an exemplary hearing with you being represented, a full team capable of investigating, defending, et cetera. As to the note you referred to, as Mr. Tieger or -- Mr. Tieger noted that they are not in the hands of the OTP, and I take it -- so it's the matter for you to pursue with the witness. So during the course of direct or cross-examination, I hope you can sort it out in one way or another. And I noted that tomorrow, there's no -- there's a courtroom vacancy, so during the course of today's hearing I'll explore, with the assistance of the Court Deputy, whether we can have an extended sitting tomorrow, and we'll do our best, and then we'll see how far we can get on with it, and then -- actually, we'll see, at the end of his evidence, whether we need to call Mr. van Lynden again or not. So that said, let's bring in the witness. Mr. Karadzic, are you minded to supplement your submission as to the sitting schedule in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber needs that, we will do so gladly, because we always objected to the rhythm involved, bearing in mind the necessity to have equality of arms. If we were to neglect all of that and if there would be a speeding up of the rhythm, then we would not have a fair trial. So if you need this in writing, if that would affect your decision, of course, I have to do that, I have to make that kind of submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is up to you whether or not to file something in supplement -- to supplement your submission. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time are you giving me for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the end of Friday. Welcome, Mr. van Lynden. If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As I told you, in this proceeding what we will be doing is entering into evidence a statement you have given, and then asking some follow-up questions. So can I ask you, please, to confirm that you've read your consolidated witness statement of 25th and 26th February of this year, that you signed on 16th of March, 2010?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you please confirm that the statement is accurate and that if you were asked questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, in the statement there were various videos referred to which are contained in the attachment to the statement. Can you confirm that these videos that you watched were accurate copies of the original broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would move to tender the consolidated statement, which is 65 ter 22289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P926. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a brief summary of the evidence. Mr. van Lynden worked as a television journalist, specialising in covering war zones. In this capacity, he covered conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, starting in 1991, on behalf of the 24-hour British news channel, Sky News. Sky News went out via satellite and could be watched throughout Europe by people who had a dish capable of receiving that station. Mr. van Lynden arrived in Sarajevo in late May of 1992, and he stayed there through September. He then spent approximately three weeks in Pale, returning in October 1992 to Sarajevo to continue his work, staying there for some time. In 1993 and 1994, Mr. van Lynden was covering conflicts elsewhere, other parts of BiH, and made shorter visits to Sarajevo. While Mr. van Lynden was in Sarajevo, he stayed mainly at the former JNA military hospital, also known as the state hospital and as the city hospital later on. The city hospital was 12 or 13 storeys high and at a fairly central location in the city, near Marin Dvor Square, the Parliament. The front-lines of Grbavica were nearby, and thus Mr. van Lynden had a crew, and his crew had a good vantage point to film from this hospital. The city hospital had been targeted for fire before Mr. van Lynden arrived there, and was fired upon during his stay there as well. While he stayed there, Mr. van Lynden did not see evidence of snipers operating from the hospital. Once he arrived in Sarajevo, Mr. van Lynden observed the conditions that the population lived under, including difficulties -- severe difficulties caused by lack of necessary resources, food, water, utilities, as well as the impact of sniping and shelling on the population of Sarajevo. In his evidence, Mr. van Lynden describes the fear which accompanied shelling and sniping attacks. He saw, on occasion, civilians who had been shot, lying in the streets of Sarajevo, and, in fact, sniping incidents became so common that unless there were unusual or aggravating features to the particular incident, it was not considered truly newsworthy. And Mr. van Lynden reported on the situation in the streets of Sarajevo, how people had to run crossing the streets at intersections for fear that they could be hit by sniper fire. He reported about sniping and heavy shelling in Sarajevo, and these stories referred to in the statement include: heavy shelling of the city and the Marsal Tito Barracks in early June 1992; more heavy shelling in June 1992 at increased intensity; firing upon the UNIS towers and other areas in Sarajevo; his observations of injured civilians being brought to the city hospital in early June; and a story from the 5th December 1992 on the firing on and burning of an apartment building in Sarajevo. Other stories and topics covered by Mr. van Lynden during this period include: the situation and conditions in Dobrinja in July 1992; his meeting with Juka Prazina in May and June of that year; a visit to Kula Prison in September 1992; a funeral of 28 VRS soldiers in Vlasenica in September 1992, which was also attended by Mr. Karadzic; and conditions he observed in Srebrenica in November 1992, when he entered the enclave. In September and October of 1992, Mr. van Lynden reported from Pale to try to cover the war from the Serb side, and while in Pale Mr. van Lynden spent several evenings with Mr. Karadzic. During these evenings, they would hold informal conversations after work in Mr. Karadzic's office, and Mr. Karadzic would take out maps, explain his view of the situation, and Mr. van Lynden stated that he could -- he observed that taking Sarajevo was an obsession for Mr. Karadzic. In September 1992, Mr. van Lynden was able to interview General Ratko Mladic. During this interview, General Mladic took Mr. van Lynden and his crew to an artillery position directly overlooking Sarajevo, and this interview was filmed. And Mr. van Lynden, looking at a map which we'll look at today, was able to identify the approximate location on this map of the firing position, where the interview was held. Following this interview with General Mladic in September 1992, Mr. van Lynden and his crew made several trips around the perimeter of Sarajevo to different Bosnian Serb positions, including Grbavica and the Jewish cemetery, where Mr. van Lynden was able to speak with the soldiers there and film the positions. He also visited Mount Trebevic, Hrasno and was taken by Bosnians to positions on Zuc Hill. In February 1993, Mr. van Lynden reported on his entry to Gorazde, where he had to walk through the foot trail overnight and spent some time there reporting on the conditions which he observed. Although there was extreme poverty, the conditions were not as dire as in Srebrenica, that he'd seen there. In February 1994, after the Markale incident, Mr. van Lynden was sent to Pale, and he filed several stories from there about negotiations for withdrawal with heavy weaponry from Sarajevo. After that agreement on the withdrawal was reached, for the first time Mr. van Lynden was able to see that one could walk across Marin Dvor Square in Sarajevo, which had been absolutely too dangerous at any other time he'd been there. Also while in Pale, Mr. van Lynden's cameraman filmed a meeting attended by Radovan Karadzic and Generals Mladic, Milovanovic, Gvero, and others, and it was at this time that General Mladic, on seeing Mr. van Lynden, grabbed him and expressed his anger about Mr. Van Lynden's reporting on Gorazde and Zuc. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you, Mr. van Lynden, just a few background questions before we go straight to Sarajevo in 1992. You were educated and born in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell me just a little bit about your military service, which I believe is with the Dutch Marines from 1976 to 1978? Did you have any specialty training?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was trained as an infantry officer and got special training as a mortar -- platoon commander and mortar platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after that military service, you became a war correspondent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell us briefly, before covering the conflict in the former Yugoslavia starting in 1991, which conflicts did you cover before that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I began by covering the conflict then already going on in Lebanon, which had begun in 1975, and I lived in Beirut from 1982 to 1986. I covered the Iran-Iraq war that began in 1980. I covered the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and made four treks into Afghanistan during the 1980s, each of them lasting around three months, on foot with the Afghan resistance. I covered the Romanian revolution in December 1989, and I covered the first Gulf war after Iraq had taken over Kuwait, and was with the allied troops during Operation Desert Storm, when Kuwait was liberated at the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I'm correct, from 1988 onwards you were working full time for Sky News?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Before that, I was largely working in newspapers and radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to talk about the bulk of your testimony here today in the time we have, and that's your experience following your arrival in Sarajevo. Do you recall when it was, in May 1992, that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Right towards the end of May, but I don't remember the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you speak about this in your statement at paragraph 6, but can you tell us what area of the Yugoslavia Sky News was broadcast over and where your reports could be received?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, our reports could be received in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, as in the whole of Europe. Anyone who had a dish that could watch the Astra satellite, on which Sky News at the time was broadcast, would be able to see the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as I - I hope I got it right - explained in the summary, you set up first -- or quickly in the former JNA military hospital, also known as the city hospital in Sarajevo. Could you tell us how you picked that location and why you chose that spot to operate from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When we drove into Sarajevo, we -- there were at that time no hotels open. Journalists in a foreign country stay in hotels, but in Sarajevo that was not, at that time, possible anymore. They had all closed or been burnt already. So I went to the Bosnian Presidency and asked them for help in finding somewhere for us to stay. We were then taken to what we were told was a building that was used in the past and during peace to house foreign VIPs, a building that later became the house in Sarajevo of the UN commander there, but at that time the UN commander wasn't there yet, and so we were housed there. It is a relatively low building, quite close to the Presidency, in the center of the city, and we had one night there. There wasn't particular heavy shelling, but there was shelling that night, and my cameraman and I noticed that we simply couldn't film this from this low building, and therefore we went on the lookout, in the days after, for a higher building from which we would be capable of filming the shelling that was taking place. As I recall, on the second or third day we went to what was then still called the military hospital, because we had heard that apart from other injured being taken care of there, there was one soldier from the then still-occupied Marsal Tito Barracks who had been taken there after being wounded, and we wanted to film and interview him and find out how that had happened. We met the chief surgeon of the hospital, Dr. Abdulah Nakas, and once we arrived at the building we saw that it had been repeated targeted already, but that it was a high building. It seemed to us a well-built building, but that -- so we asked him to see the higher floors and what we might be able to film from there. The upper floors of the hospital had been evacuated. They were no longer considered safe for patients, so it was an empty floor. We went to the top floor, and we asked Dr. Nakas if, in future, we would be able to stay there during the nights to film the fighting when it took place. The building had two different things that made it interesting for us. Firstly, it was high and had a good view of much of the city. There was a little left-hand balcony. You could film from there the old part of Sarajevo. Right in front was Marin Dvor Square, the Parliament building, and the southern hills of Sarajevo, and to the right there was another little balcony from which -- so we could film the new part of Sarajevo. So it was a vantage point. We asked Dr. Nakas. He was very surprised that we should want to live on the top floor of a building that had already been repeatedly targeted. But he gave his consent, and after that, that's where we stayed practically every single night when we were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you make any inquiries or check to see whether that building was being used by Bosnian forces and whether any sniping activity took place from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we immediately did. If you go to a building that has been repeatedly and very clearly targeted and hit, you also wonder why. And as the correspondent with a television crew, I am responsible -- or I was responsible for the well-being, as far as possible in a war zone, of that crew. Therefore, if I'm going to go into a building, I'm going to check whether it is actually a building that is being used by military forces, and we checked quite carefully. I had already, from my experience in 1991 in the former Yugoslavia, noticed that Yugoslav soldiers of whatever their nationality or religious background were usually not very careful in tidying up after themselves, and therefore it seemed likely to us that if there had been snipers in that building, we would find empty cartridge cases. That was not the case. We even went on the roof at night, which is dangerous because then you are a silhouette. We found absolutely nothing there. We found nothing on the lower floors. And in all our conversations, because we did ask other people as well, no one ever said that that building had been used for military purposes by the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you were there, staying there from the end of May/early June onwards, was the hospital targeted and hit by fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to the extent you can tell, what type of weapons or projectiles were used to target the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's a difficult question to answer. If you are in a building that is hit, it's not always immediately possible to know, A, the size of the hit, sound levels, when you're in one part and another part is hit. However, while I was in the building, most of it seemed of smaller calibre, sometimes maybe 20, 30, or 40-millimetre which can be fired from anti-aircraft guns, and only on one occasion that I was in the building, and that I clearly recall, were we fairly certain that it had been a tank shell or something of that nature, because it was an extremely heavy detonation and it hit part of the lift shaft within the building, destroying that particular lift shaft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to show you a photo, a panoramic photograph of Sarajevo. This is 65 ter 14665A. Your Honours, this is the -- this is a photograph which I would -- the one exhibit which I added to my list and filed a notification about. Now, what we can see on the bottom is 14665, and we've just blown up part of the center of the photo. On the top portion of the photo, Mr. van Lynden -- no, that's a little bit too big. If we can -- if we can zoom out a bit. Can we just -- yeah. Are you able to see where the state -- the former military hospital that you stayed in is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the right-hand side. It's the white building on the right-hand side of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could somebody assist Mr. van Lynden? I'd like him to mark this with a stylus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you perhaps just draw an arrow to the building and mark that as -- with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see and point out the UNIS towers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you able to mark the Parliament building or point towards it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Number 3, thank you. Could you also mark the Holiday Inn, if you see it there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 4, thank you. That's number 4. And number 5, could you just mark -- this is not a photo from 1992. This is a more recent photo. Could you please mark the location of the Marsal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, it's quite a large complex, but it was roughly here [marks] behind these flags. So that would be number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P927. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you some questions, now that we've established where you were staying and how you picked the spot, about what you observed of daily life and the conditions for the population of Sarajevo after you arrived. This is mainly in paragraphs 21 to 30 of the consolidated statement. Can you just briefly tell us, in your own words, when you arrived, your impression of what conditions the citizens were living under in terms of their access to food, water, necessary utilities? Just briefly give us what you recall.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that made a very clear impression on us is that we crossed, by road, from Ilidza, which was held by the Bosnian Serbs, into the territory held by the Bosnian government, and it was that there was no one on the roads. At that time, the Marsal Tito Barracks were still in the hands of the JNA, and, therefore, we had to take a convoluted road around the hills to get to the central part of Sarajevo. You saw practically no vehicle on the road. If you did, they were driving at extremely high speed. It was sometimes on the roads as if it was a ghost town. If you saw people on roads that were in sight of the Bosnian-held territory on the southern hills overlooking Sarajevo, people ran. I mean, apart from sometimes the old, who were incapable of running but still had to cross the street, everybody ran across the streets. It wasn't, at the time when we arrived, that there was heavy gun-fire going on continually. There was occasional gun-fire. But wherever you were in these districts, where people were not under cover and where they felt they were under threat of gun-fire, people ran across the streets. I've never been in a city before -- and I lived in Beirut, which was a city of war, but it didn't have that kind of situation where, in such a large part of the city, the only way people could cross the street was at speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As far as the other question of electricity, gas, water supplies, and food was concerned, there were no shops open by the time we reached Sarajevo at the end of May 1992. They were empty. There were small markets where individuals sold whatever produce. At that time, it was still possible, for instance, in Sarajevo to buy bottles of red wine. They would run out pretty quickly. But there were just a few vegetables, very little on the market, and so food was already a problem for the population. Electricity, at the end of May 1988 -- 1992, was not such a problem, yet at later stages of the war most areas of Sarajevo would not have electricity. And as far as gas and water supplies, as far as I'm aware, again, those problems would be much worse and exacerbated later on, but in that stage -- early stage of the war, people, I think, generally still had water supplies at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to play a short video-clip now. This is 65 ter 40264A, broadcast, it should be, on the 1st of June. And if we can stop, Mr. Reid, right at the beginning where we see the symbol. All right. We're stopped at 00:00:06:8, showing a computerised screen with the date on it. Can you just tell us, because we may see more of these, Mr. van Lynden, what does this screen at the beginning of your broadcast mean?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These are put before a story by the central office in London, because they go into a computerised machine so that the programme editors can run the stories when they want to. There is a line-up clock of 40 seconds beforehand, and after the two seconds -- we stopped two seconds before the picture will begin, it shows firstly at the top a slug, which is the name of the story, in this case, my first name, "Aernout" and "Yugo," as in Yugoslavia. "PGM" means the programme, so it was the 1800 show that this story went out on on the day, the Monday, and then on the date, the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, for your reference, this is a video referenced in paragraph 44 of the statement. Could we play the clip now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "In Sarajevo, the cross roads can be lethal, needed to be taken at speed. They and the avenues that cut across the city offer the Serb gunners in the hills above with open lines of fire, prime targets which the old and infirm are forced to accept as the new, uncomfortable realities of life. As the people of Sarajevo scurry across their streets, the latest cease-fire is being proposed and agreed at a meeting --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There, we can stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, these -- first of all, I think this is the first story, was it not, that you sent out after arriving in Sarajevo in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The scene that's been captured there of the people hurrying across the streets and the intersections, you started to talk about it, but was that the norm or the exception? Was that something difficult to find to film or could you just explain how prevalent that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was the norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you started talking about it as well, but in paragraph 46 of your statement you talked about how Sarajevo was very different from Beirut and your experience in Beirut. And we saw, in this short clip that we played before we stopped at 00:45:4, a shot from the hills overlooking Sarajevo. It was straight down to the intersection. Could you explain to us about those lines of fire and how Sarajevo was different, in your view, from Beirut?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that one has to understand about Sarajevo is that it's the city built around a river at the bottom of the valley, the River Miljacka, and then it has hills rising up from that valley floor to the south and to the north. What you saw there were the hills to the south which were held by the Bosnian Serbs, and it literally meant, and we were to see that ourselves when -- in September 1992, when we worked on the Bosnian Serb side and filmed it from that side, that those there could literally look down a street from above onto the various streets and intersections of the city of Sarajevo, the heart of Sarajevo, on the valley floor below them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you say those there could look down at the valley floors, is that who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: To the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, could we give that video a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P928. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just briefly you discuss in paragraph 26 of your statement one particular sniping incident, where you stated you did not witness the people actually being shot and the impact of the bullet, but saw them in the streets. Afterwards, in the attempt to rescue them, can you for us, just as an illustration, describe what you saw on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was, as I recall it, July of 1992. We had been at the TV station and were driving back from the TV station along Marsal Tito Boulevard, and we had just about reached or were just before what had been the Marsal Tito Barracks when we were stopped by people on the road, and then we stopped. And then we saw that there were a number of people lying in the street. This is a broad street, and they had been shot while trying to cross this street. As I recall it, there were three people. They were all still alive, but they had been seriously wounded. We were told that first one person had been shot and wounded, a second person had run out to help them, and that person had been shot, and then it happened with a third person. After that, people had got the message and decided not to run out there anymore. And they finally waited until, as I recall, a blue-painted armoured -- wheeled armoured car, what must have been the police forces, came to position itself between those bodies and the position from which the fire had emanated, which was the southern part of Beirut -- of Sarajevo. My apologies. This took some time, and when the armoured vehicle came, there was further fire on the three people lying in the street. As I recall, at least two out of three were killed. They were then -- the bodies were then put into the armoured vehicle and driven off. We drove after the vehicle, and I recall that we actually went into the mortuary of Kosevo Hospital, the academic hospital of Sarajevo, where the bodies were brought, and were there, in rather too graphic a manner, shown how these people had been killed. As I recall it, the man in the mortuary actually put his finger into -- through the bullet hole of one of the dead people to show the trajectory of the bullet that had killed this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember if these were men or women?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember if these were men or women, the victims?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, one woman and two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just as far as you could tell, were these civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were definitely civilians. By that stage, most of the soldiers on the Bosnian side were wearing uniform. They were not wearing uniform. As I recall it, the woman who was shot had a shopping bag with her and was roughly middle-aged. No, we were -- we asked, also, but as far as we were told, these were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I referred to in my opening short summary of your evidence, at one point in paragraph 49 of your statement you say that the sniping incidents became so common that individual incidents were not newsworthy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm afraid to say that it is. When it first begins in a war, if I can draw the parallel, it is like the suicide bombings in Iraq today. They may have been first point of the news during 2003, but today hardly get a mention, while they do continue. With Sarajevo, that was the case with the sniping incidents. The early stage of the war, when this was still something completely new, that the city that had hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics was coming under sniper fire, where civilians were being shot at, that changed, even by the summer of 1992, after just a few months, that sniping incidents became much less newsworthy. There were occasions when that was not the case. There was one incident of a young man and a woman who tried to flee from Sarajevo, and it was a kind of Romeo and Juliet story of a Muslim and an Orthodox, and they were both shot dead. That was something that took a lot of international attention. By on the whole, by this stage of the war already, the international media was not paying that much attention to such individual sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to June 1992 and the stories you filed in early -- in the first weeks of June. And this, Your Honours, concerns paragraphs 52 to 58, primarily, of the consolidated statement, the shelling and targeting of the city. And I noted in the filing Monday, Your Honour, there was a typo in the statement. At paragraph 52, footnote 14, we had the wrong 65 ter number. The correct is 40264C, a video, and I'd like to play that now. This is from the 5th of June, according to the slug at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember that you noted the correct one should be D.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: D. I may have misspoke, Your Honour. D is correct. Thank you. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marsal Tito Barracks --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. If we can stop. I want to play a different one first. It is 4264C. My apologies. I'll play this one in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "... dusk in Sarajevo. Amongst the city's ancient minarets, the rockets fall, heralding another night of heavy shelling."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Switch off microphones in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "For the next six hours, there is no let-up. Eerily lit up by flares, the city is hit from every side by practically every imaginable projectile. Long lines of heavy machine-gun fire gliding across the roofs, exploding against their targets. Heavy shells slamming into buildings, within seconds engulfing them in flames. A mass of crazy sparks lighting the brow of one hill from a quick-fire volley of mortar bombs. "This is the scene of wholesale devastation, of a city being obliterated while the world watches, but does nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this video we just watched, on the front, the computerised date had the 5th of June. We can see quite clearly what you were able to film, but could you just tell us what are we seeing here? Which areas of the city, if you recall, were you filming in this clip and at that time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: All these images were taken from our position within the military hospital, as I described at the beginning of the session here. The first pictures were taken from the balcony, what we called the left, overlooking the old part of Sarajevo. You see a rocket. It's a rocket fired from the top of the hill to the east of Sarajevo, landing on the old part of Sarajevo. What you see later is filmed either from the middle windows overlooking the central part of Sarajevo or on the right-hand balcony, of shells, heavy machine-gun fire, going into the newer part of Sarajevo. This fire is all emanated from south of Sarajevo, from the hill-sides south. You could see it coming down on the city. The whole city was basically being targeted. It wasn't one specific target that was being hit or one particular district of the city being hit. This was fire that was coming down all across the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, that short clip that we saw ending at 09:28:8, it's a difficult question, but how much of the shelling that night were you able to capture on that short clip? How much does that represent? And I'll ask you a follow-up question in a minute. If you could just tell us about how much you were able to get that we saw there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The first thing I should explain to anyone who's not been in a war zone, working for television, is that filming that kind of thing is extremely difficult, because you hear a bang and it's over there, and by the time you get there, of course, the bang has already happened, and you may see some smoke, but at night that's even more difficult. And then you think, Well, maybe I should focus the camera there, and then it happens on the other side. For a film crew, therefore, to get quite this much, and not only that night but several other nights after that, to capture that much firing, it means there was much, much more. There were moments -- and the cameraman who was with me was also the cameraman who had been with me in the Gulf war, in the Romanian revolution, and throughout 1991, during the war in Croatia. We had never been able to capture such footage of fighting or of artillery. It should give an indication that this was really an extremely heavy night of shelling, as were the nights that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just give us an idea of how long this shelling would go on for; in other words, when it would start in the evening and how late into the night or into the morning it would continue?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, that differed from day to day. On these pictures you see, they were still daylight pictures that we began with, so that would have been towards the end of the afternoon, the early evening. As I recall, that night it went on until 3.00, 4.00 in the morning, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to -- Sorry, Your Honours. Could I please give this an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what we saw just now is D, not C, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that was C, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was C, thank you. Yes, it will be given the number of P292?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction, Your Honours. It will be given Exhibit P929. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you already spoke a little bit today about the Marsal Tito Barracks and the situation there. I want to play another video now, which is 65 ter 40264D from 6 June, which concerns the barracks and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marsal Tito Barracks, it becomes the night's prime target. The shells land long, around Sarajevo's railway yard. But inside the vast army complex those still looking for loot get the message and run. Not long after, the gunners in the hills above the Bosnian capital find their range. The barracks explode in flames. The barracks form the principal target, yet no district escapes. Through the dark, the rockets streak down, for a moment illuminating Sarajevo's ancient centre, before reducing it to further rubble. They come in ones, in twos, in threes, and it sounds as if the city's crying. "At 3.00 in the morning, the barracks are again bearing the full weight of attention. Whole wings of this vast, if not deserted military complex are in flame. With light, the people rarely come out to inspect the damage."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've stopped now at 12.53:2, at the point where the video shows people carrying a bed out of a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what we saw there in the beginning, when you discussed in the broadcast the gunners finding their range, and at the beginning we can see shells hitting near the railroad tracks?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is normal for all artillery or mortar units that when they are given a specific target to fire on, that they will initially probably have shells landing too long or too short. What we witnessed there was the initial shells falling too long, falling over the Marsal Tito Barracks and hitting the railway yard behind it, to the north of the barracks, and then they found their range. This is what happens with artillery units and mortar units throughout the world. They go too far, they go too short, and then they hit it and they continue to hit it. On this occasion, there was extremely -- after those initial shells, there was extremely accurate fire throughout that night on the Marsal Tito Barracks, whole parts of which, indeed, burnt. That's what you saw right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what do we see later on? Is it the same kind of fire or is it all Marsal Tito, or what's happening afterwards on that clip?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What you see after that is that whilst the Marsal Tito Barracks was being directly targeted, simultaneously all other districts of the city were being targeted as well, and there in an often much more haphazard fashion, again, Your Honours, making it much more difficult for us to film, because one or two rockets would come down in one part of the city, and then it would stop there, at least for some time, and we would have to go from one part of the hospital -- from one side to the other side because the fire was coming down on the other side. It was much more haphazard fire on the other parts, never as concentrated as we saw on the Marsal Tito Barracks. When I was with the British and American forces in the Gulf war in the lead-up to the ground campaign to liberate Kuwait, I spent quite a lot of time with artillery units. I'm not an artillerist, I wasn't trained in this, and I asked them about what they were planning and how they were planning the actual operation right at the beginning of the ground campaign to liberate Kuwait. They explained to me that they would be given specific targets, that you would get this kind of shooting, and that with all their targets there would be a follow-up of military personnel on the ground; tanks, armoured vehicle, infantry attack on that target following the initial artillery barrage. What we saw here, there was absolutely nothing happening as far as infantry was concerned. This was purely a barrage on the Marsal Tito Barracks, but also on the city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we give that a number, please, Your Honours. That was D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P930. In addition, just one thing for the record. There is no surrogate sheet for this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now a question and look at the video about the story about the UNIS towers, which is referred to in paragraph 59 of the statement. Your Honours, am I right that we have five minutes to the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We could -- we could continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to play this video now, which is 40264E, from the 7th of June, according to the code on the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "It was the symbol of modern Sarajevo, now of its destruction. Flames tear across the floors and up into the higher storeys, showering debris onto the streets at the heart of the Bosnian capital, the disintegration of one of the city's UNIS towers reflected in the broken windows of its twin. "Three hundred metres on across the road, the Parliament of this newly-independent state is also struck. It doesn't burn, but the nearby Marsal Tito Barracks do. Since its evacuation two days earlier, it's been systematically destroyed. "Every night in Sarajevo, you think it can't get worse, but it does, making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to this city which is enfolded in war. "Less than 24 hours earlier, the Serb commanders had put their signatures on yet another agreement, affirming a truce never adhered to and their readiness to reopen the airport. Now the Serb gunners in the hills show where their true commitment lies. Under a sickle moon, the city rocks to the explosions. Lit up by fire and the mass of glowing sparks that drift across its roofs. "Daylight, we find the intensive care wards of the city's central hospital packed, with amputees in pain. Some will live, but the doctors are resigned to this girl's death. Not far from where she lies, do others that have gone before. A place of haphazard death, some covered, some not, where maggots crawl the floors. A little house of Bosnian horror. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you -- I think the clip and your narration was pretty self-explanatory, but can you tell us what you know about who this person in the last shot is, the young boy lying on the table, or what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He wasn't lying on a table. He was lying on a stretcher on the floor. He was a young boy, as you say. And from what we'd gathered, he'd been killed by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we give that a number, please, Your Honour. That was 40264E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this shall be given Exhibit P931. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last question on that video about the UNIS towers, Mr. van Lynden. Were you able to notice or did you see whether there was any fire coming from the UNIS towers at the time that it was being hit?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I never witnessed fire coming from the UNIS towers, no. We went into the UNIS towers several days earlier, because this was when the Marsal Tito Barracks was still occupied by the JNA, and we wanted -- it was a high position so we could film into the Marsal Tito Barracks. We wanted to open the window, and we couldn't. They were fixed windows. It had an air-conditioning system. And, therefore, unless one broke a window in there, it would not have made a perfect firing ground. That's the first thing. The second thing is during the time -- relatively few days, it's true that we had been in the hospital, we had seen the UNIS towers every single day, and we never saw any fire emanating from there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to continue now to play another video, this one from the first screen shot of 9 June, 1992. It's 40264F, is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Sarajevo's burning, in its heart and in its suburbs. Suddenly, on Sunday night the whole city becoming the target, no district spared, all shaking as every 10 seconds the rocket shells and mortars land, the fire so heavy, so incessant, that the deadly streams of light criss-cross each other. By early Monday morning, the inundation of the hospitals begins. The doctors and the nurses of the city's former military hospital already up throughout the night, at the beginning of a dark, grim day, the like of which they've never known; trained fingers which, for 24 hours will work without respite to stem blood, extract jagged metal, preserve life. But so many casualties of war, so many distorted faces and torn limbs. "At the city's main hospital, the situation is even worse. The counter-offensive of the Bosnian territorial defence forces have run into a continual barrage from the heavy guns that surround them, the costs enormous, and the stream of casualties is now incessant. "This is a scene of utter mayhem. No minute passes without a new van or ambulance coming in bearing more wounded. The battle of Sarajevo has reached a peak. Countless young men on stretches raging against the dying of the light, and so many who've lost that struggle that they lie outside a morgue already over-full. "Across the town, in its modern center, a new fire rages just by the front-line. Somehow, the firemen make it, but their efforts are futile. They're impotent as the water is cut. All they can do is stand and watch. Fifty yards away, others fight on from behind the cover of a devastated urban battleground, small groups of men answering artillery with small arms. "As evening falls, the city is marked by tens of fires, and inside its surviving walls, by pain and endurance, by faces marked by fear, shock, and sheer fatigue. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that video-clip, we saw in the beginning, again, more shelling, and you said words to the effect of the whole city becoming a target. Can you tell us just, as you remember, which areas of the city that night were shelled, or which districts?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I said, it was our impression that the whole city came under fire. We did not see the same sustained fire that we had seen on one particular target, as with the Marsal Tito Barracks, at which time other parts of the city had also been hit, but that night the whole city seemed to be the target. And it was our impression that this was done to simply terrorise those still living in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then later on in the morning film, there were soldiers being brought in from a counter-offensive. Can you just tell us, briefly, what we were seeing there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was -- this was a separate matter. This -- from what we were given to understand, at a certain area around what had once been the maternity hospital of Sarajevo, the Bosnian Army had launched some kind of a counter-offensive to push back the Serb lines in that area, and there was very heavy fighting going on, and many of those men were wounded and killed. And as far as I'm aware, that offensive didn't work. It was -- it was not successful. But that should be held separate to the pictures that we took during the night, the preceding night, of the entire city coming under shell fire. Those were two separate things. While that battle was going on during the day, there was fire into the city as well, but not nearly as heavily as there had been during the night, and the fighting was very much concentrated in that one district slightly to the north of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, just very briefly, you talk about this in paragraph 59, but what ethnicities did you see being brought into -- I'm not talking specifically about this incident, but when you observed people -- injured people being brought into the hospital you stayed at, and other hospitals, which ethnicities were they? Was it simply Muslim Bosniak or others as well?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I'm aware, they were all Slavs, which I think is the same ethnicity. They had different religions. We were told, and we asked those who were capable of speech, those who had been wounded, what they were, and what we got was that most of them were Muslim, but there were also Catholics, what people would call Croats, and Orthodox Bosnian Serbs amongst those soldiers that were wounded. Throughout the war, wherever I was in Bosnia, I encountered Bosnian Serbs in the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move now to what's contained in paragraph 62, the portion of your statement where you talk about the story you did on Dobrinja. I'm not going to show that story now, but could you just tell us -- clarify for me one point from paragraph 62. You say: "During the initial stages of the war," and we're speaking now of July 1992, "that Dobrinja had a separate siege to the rest of Sarajevo." Could you just tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Could I just have the screen back so I could see what is being said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can ask the question again, and in a better way, as well, hopefully. What was -- what is meant by "the separate siege of Dobrinja"?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Dobrinja is the western suburb of Sarajevo, built close to the airport, to house the athletes for the 1984 Winter Olympic Games. After that, it became an area where I believe mostly young couples were able to get apartments. It's slightly separate, and that area was -- the whole of Dobrinja wasn't in Bosnian government hands, but a large part of it was, and the Bosnian Serbs controlled a hill called Mojmilo Hill, which was really the connection between Dobrinja and the rest of the city, and thereby they made it impossible for there to be a direct connection between the two different parts, Sarajevo proper and the suburb of Dobrinja, and, therefore, there was a form of separate siege. You couldn't drive to Dobrinja, and that only became possible when, in July, the forces of the Bosnian government within Dobrinja took Mojmilo Hill. After that, a direct connection was made between this western suburb and the city proper. And we were able to get in there, but it was a very dangerous drive. We were the first journalists to go in. We were told that five other cars had tried to make that journey during the day, and all five had been hit by Serb gun-fire. We did manage to go there. We were there for 48 hours and then drove out again, and both when we drove in and when we drove out, we did come under gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honours, with the last exhibit, 40264F, the video we just saw, I neglected to ask for that to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Exhibit P932.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm now going to move, Mr. van Lynden, to September 1992 and your time in Pale, and first ask you, just very briefly, how you came to go to Pale. And, Your Honours, this is -- the area I'm going into now is principally in paragraphs 65 to 90 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to explain how I first came to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask you a question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, from the statement, that you'd met with Mr. Karadzic in June 1992 in Pale, and then in August 1992 in London, and then in September 1992 in Belgrade. And if you can just explain briefly how those meetings resulted in your being able to report from Pale.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When we had first gone to Sarajevo towards the end of May 1992, we had gone from Belgrade and driven to Pale. It was decided by Sky management -- we had a satellite dish to be able to send the stories back to London with us. They felt at that time it was not safe to take it into Sarajevo, so that was left in Pale, at the Pension Olympic. I didn't at that time meet Mr. Karadzic, but I then drove into the city. Our stories were sent from Pale, and when we at a certain moment left Sarajevo and we returned to Pale, because we needed to send our material out of the city. That was in June. We then tried to work for a number of days out of Pale to try and cover the war from the other side. This is when I briefly met Mr. Karadzic. And that turned out to be practically impossible, because every time we set out from the hotel in Pale and went to further areas, we would be arrested at various check-points. My bosses in London then decided to withdraw me for a time, and I went back to London and later returned to Sarajevo. When at the August conference that was held in London, I had the opportunity to meet Mr. Karadzic, and asked him for his help in returning to Pale and being able to actually work from Pale so that we could cover their side of the story and to allow the Bosnian Serbs to speak for themselves. He agreed that we should hold a meeting in Belgrade. When I got there at the beginning of September, a meeting was held at the Intercontinental Hotel, as I recall. Mr. Karadzic arranged for an escort from Belgrade to take us to Pale. Once we were in Pale, we met him again, as we did several times during that stay there, and he then arranged for two military policemen to be given as a permanent escort for us to be able to work on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you get any kind of letter of authorisation or letter of credentials from the Bosnian Serb authorities to show that you were able to work there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this was after a conversation with Mr. Karadzic, and we were given a letter the next day; not signed by him, but signed by Mr. Krajisnik, who was the speaker of the Bosnian Serb Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you discuss, in paragraphs 69 to 75 of your statement, that you had several informal -- not formal interviews, but informal meetings with Mr. Karadzic while you were in Pale, and that you would discuss various topics, and I'm going to ask about that now. But, first of all, where would you meet Mr. Karadzic when you had these meetings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We met him at his office, apart from on one occasion when we were at the television station and he was there as well, and we then got into a conversation there with him and with several of the people working at TV Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us what that was about? That's another topic, but since we're there, what was going on at the TV station?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We would go to the TV station to be able to send our stories, which then went from Pale to Belgrade, and from Belgrade they were up-linked and sent to London. When we were there on that particular evening, an argument broke out. A number of those people working at TV Pale attacked me for my coverage from Sarajevo, my previous coverage from Sarajevo, in particular for a story I had done about a certain Bosnian called Jusuf Prazina. They felt that I had made him look like a hero, while I think in the story I had made quite perfectly clear that this man had been in jail and was a convicted criminal. Mr. Karadzic slightly intervened in this conversation. The conversation also ranged about other matters, but it was, for me, an example of the strange mentality that seemed to have most people in their grip in Pale, that a story about a man who I described as one of the principal defenders of Sarajevo in that story done at the beginning of June, Jusuf Prazina, who I mentioned was a convicted criminal, that they felt that this was a story that was against them. And they never mentioned any of the other stories of Sarajevo being shelled, as we've just seen the stories that you have just shown the Court, or held those stories against me. It was the Prazina story. And I said, This is the inverted world. A story that's actually in your interests, you attack me for. The stories that you might have attacked me for because they are not in your interests, you think are fine. It struck me as very odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I won't go through, because it's in your statement, everything about these meetings, but in paragraph 73 you talk about, at one point, that Karadzic, talking about Sarajevo, made a reference to a Berlin wall being built there to divide the city. Could you just tell us about -- briefly about that conversation and what Karadzic -- his views that he expressed to you were about living with the other people in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, this was a conversation at the end of the evening, quite late, around 11.00. And we were offered a glass of wine, and, as I recall, he was drinking white wine, and he showed us maps. He said that, in his view, Sarajevo was actually a Serb city, belonged to the Serbs, it was Serb territory, and that he made the point repeatedly that it was impossible to live with these people, and that he said a wall, that could be one of the solutions. I'm not sure that it was the -- that he said that was the only solution, but one of the solutions that he offered was that a wall should be built between the Serb parts and those of the other communities living in Sarajevo. I found that a fairly outrageous comment, because this was made less than three years after the fall of the Berlin Wall, which was a symbol of the divisions of Europe, which had finally ended. And to make a suggestion to build a wall in a city to divide people in this manner in Europe at the end of the 20th century, I found totally unacceptable, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And one other point, I just want to make it very -- ask you a follow-up question. In paragraph 71 of the statement, you talk about Dr. Karadzic telling you that the Serbs had to have the northern areas and Banja Luka, and that he said that Eastern Bosnia was all Serb: "He told me that the enclaves were unacceptable, that they had to become part of Serb territory." Now, in this conversation in September 1992, which area was under discussion when we -- when he said, These enclaves are unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The enclaves of Gorazde, Srebrenica, and then you had a number of smaller enclaves. I don't know -- I cannot recall whether every single one was precisely named, but the Eastern Bosnian enclaves were something that everybody understood, and that he felt that they -- not only were they nonviable in an economic sense, but that they were a thorn in the side of the Bosnian Serbs and that thorn should be removed. He made that quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to move on - this is contained in paragraphs, again, 76 to 90 - and ask you some questions about your interview with General Ratko Mladic in September 1992. And can you briefly tell us, how was this interview set up? How did you get permission or arrange to interview General Mladic? Who did you ask for that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was done by speaking to Mr. Karadzic and through his office. There was -- I think he was a lawyer, a Bosnian Serb, who was working for Mr. Karadzic, whom we spoke to on a daily basis. We didn't speak to Mr. Karadzic on a daily basis. And we had asked, really, on arrival in Pale whether we would be allowed to have an interview with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to play the video of that interview now. That's 40259B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "... the scourge of Sarajevo, the chief warrior of the Serbs. He's called Ratko Mladic. Appropriately, Ratko means warrior, and this squared-jouled Serb general has lived up to the name. Commander always on the move, a visit to one of the mountain's chalets where the Serbs of Bosnia have established their separatist government is but a fleeting one. In a short briefing, the Commander-in-Chief speaks only of attacks on his forces, never of offensives by them. And as if to prove the point, he gives us the rare chance to accompany him to front-line artillery positions where the UN observers are conspicuous by their absence. "High up on the windswept hills, the 100-millimetre guns are dug deep into the rocks directly overlooking Sarajevo, an overwhelming position of strength which is obviously to the general's satisfaction, as he says he holds the city in his palm, and many of the buildings in the haze below bear testimony to that power. Yet General Mladic is quite unrepentant. He is a man who has no doubts, only a total assurance that he's right, the world wrong, and that his people have been slandered. [Voice-over] "I hope that the Security Council first takes measures too understand that we Serbs are a reality in this world, not some sort of extra terrestrials, and that we have the right to defend ourselves. "Nearby, more positions are being dug. In the general's eyes, the world may deny his people their rights, but that's not going to stop him. [Voice-over] "We have to fight as long as we continue to exist to defend ourselves. There is no other way, and we're prepared for a long war. "Far away from the battle-field, the UN is preparing a resolution on war crimes. It leaves Ratko Mladic quite unmoved. [Voiceover] "I'm not bothered at all. I did not take part in any crimes, I have only defended my people. "With that, the general departs to inspect other front-lines in a war neither he, nor his officers, believe will end any time soon. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, on the front-lines outside Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we perhaps give that a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P933. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions about the video we just saw. In the video, you described buildings visible in the haze below, but on the video we just saw in court, it was difficult to see anything other than a sort of white cloud. At the time -- well, can you just tell us how visible the city was below at the time that you were actually there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, you could see the city and you could see -- in the original pictures, you could see the city. The pictures have been copied too often, and the quality has clearly reached a stage which you can't. But while there was a haze over Sarajevo, you could clearly see the city straight below that artillery position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any restrictions put on you about what you could film when you came to this artillery position?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
