utterances.text: No, we were allowed to film, only on -- right at the end, when the general left, the cameraman followed the general and his party leaving, and they walked past the cemetery. And this was clearly also that the cameraman got that in his shot, and we were then asked not to include that shot in the story that we filed to London. But that's -- in any war zone, television teams are usually asked to be very careful not to -- so that you don't give away the position to the enemy. So that is a reasonable request, although the filming was so open of the position that we were that anyone watching in Sarajevo should pretty much have been able to work out where that position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with that, could I show you P00914. That, Your Honours, I should say, is the same as P00842, a map which was on my list, but it's a slightly larger section of the map that's simply blown up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know how clear the map is to you, Mr. van Lynden, but are you able to locate the approximate position of the interview on here? And if you could --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And just to be very clear, that's -- from looking at this map and being at the interview and filming from that spot, you believe that's the approximate location of the interview with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's to the east of the city, looking from the east over the whole city, so it would have been roughly up there on the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if I could give this a number as marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I forgot to ask the witness to put the date and signature. Could you do that at the end of -- in the right bottom part of the map, could you put the date of today, the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. If we can store this and then exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P934. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were there at the position with General Mladic and his escorts, did you see an indication that this position was vulnerable to fire from the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was high up -- a high-up position. If the opposition had artillery of their own, then it would have been vulnerable, yes. Any other way, no. It was too far away from the front-lines, so it was certainly not vulnerable. If the Bosnian Army had had heavy artillery in Sarajevo, then they could have fired back on that position. I saw no indication that there had ever been any fire on that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's in your -- could you tell us how the next time you saw General Mladic and ran into him, if he had any reaction to this story or if you could see that he had actually heard about or watched the story?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The initial reaction in Pale by certain people, certainly at TV Pale, was fairly negative to this story, specifically for the opening line that I used for that story, which was, "He's the scourge [Realtime transcript read in error 'courage'] of Sarajevo." They felt that that was a negative comment on my part. General Mladic, himself, whom we encountered by chance on the road three or four days later, stopped and said, Hello, and with a big smile on his face, in Serbo-Croat said, I'm the scourge of Sarajevo, and clapped me on my shoulder, and then said -- invited us to come and have lunch with him. He was driving to a certain base, and we went with him and had lunch with him and his forces there. And he certainly didn't feel that the comment that I had made was in any sense negative. In fact, he seemed rather proud of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should note that, for the record, the transcript should read "scourge" instead of "courage."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't switched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 88 of your statement, you say that it's not on the interview, but you asked General Mladic if it would be possible to visit his troops in other positions. Can you just briefly tell us, and then I'll ask you about a couple of them, which areas from the Serb positions you were able to visit after this interview?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We had also asked Mr. Karadzic, obviously, and it was -- it was possible. We were taken to positions on Mount Trebevic and down into Sarajevo, in Grbavica and certain Serb positions in Hrasno. Later on, we were taken right the way 'round Sarajevo by a road that had been constructed clearly after the beginning of the siege, passed Vogosca and to Ilidza. There, it was not always possible for us to work. Local commanders, despite the fact that we had an escort of two Serb military policemen and the letter from Mr. Krajisnik, as I mentioned earlier, local commanders sometimes refused to let us film or refused to even speak to us. And we went to Hadzici, and close to Hadzici we were allowed to film at a certain front-line position. So at Hadzici -- but specifically where we did most of the filming, was when we went to Mount Trebevic, to Grbavica and Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not going to play the Grbavica video now, and it's discussed in your statement, but I will go to the next one, 65 ter 40259D, which is a story on one of these positions you visited. This is in paragraphs 102 to 103 of the statement. If we could watch that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "They still sing of amazing grace at Sarajevo's Catholic convent, but the pews are practically empty. Just five nuns have stayed on in the building literally overlooking the front-lines of the war. That and the food shortages hamper their work, although Sister Matila [phoen] still brings a meal each day to an elderly Serb labourer. "The Convent of the Sisters of Little Jesus is one of the very few havens in an areas which, even by Sarajevo's standards, is notorious for the ferocity of its war. "The no-man's land that has given the area its name is the Jewish cemetery, across the jumble of graves, new and old, some of the fiercest battles have been fought. The string of little villas lining the cemetery have been turned into bunkers, sitting-room walls roughly redecorated with lines of logs, although some of the defences are more imaginative; bathroom mirrors subtly deployed to allow one guard to view all angles. Of late, the tanks against the Serb lines in this sector have diminished, leaving the battalion commander exuding confidence. [Voiceover] "We're ready for a long struggle, but we believe we will only spend a short time in these positions. Either they will have to accept peace or there will be all-out war, in which we will try to achieve victory in a very short time. "The major's confidence is understandable, unlike his opponents he doesn't face a lack of logistical support made worse by siege. And if he is ordered to attack, he will do so from a commanding position, so commanding that in the streets below few dare to move. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at the end there, from that VRS position we could see shots of the street below, but I just wanted to ask: Were those actually shots taken from that position by the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That, I don't think -- no, I think they were pictures taken from a slightly different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. But they're from the position that we're seeing in the story where your talking, or are they from --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The positions at the Jewish cemetery are lower down. These would be slightly higher up. It would be fairly close and probably in the same area that this battalion commander who you saw, the major that I mentioned and that we saw in the picture, had under his command, but they were filmed at different position. I mean, the building you saw at the end is the parliamentary building, and the streets are in that part, I mean, Bosnian-held Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we give that video a number, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P935. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I now want to go to the last video which I'll play today, and that is 65 ter 40267, which is from the 5th of December, I believe, or approximately that date, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "... burned four days after the Serbs launched their offensive, Sarajevo's wester suburb falls into their hands. For months, the defenders of Sarajevo have tried to break the siege. Now it's being tightened another notch. By morning, only small pockets of resistance remain, yet the shelling continues, unchanged, incessant. Those who can escape. Those who can't face almost certain death. For the UN forces here and for the politicians who sent them, the latest fighting marks yet another humiliation, making a mockery of peace-making efforts. For a change, they admit as much. "We are not making any progress at all. The situation is deteriorating. I can't see any progress. And all of the Security Council's resolutions, all of these [indiscernible] agreements, all of these effort we are making here to improve the situation and to save the lives and to restore the capability of the utilities for the winter is completely failed, and we move one -- one step forward and we find ourselves two steps back. "Words mirrored by the reality in the city. Serb incendiary rounds setting a string of flats ablaze in one apartment block. A resident watches, distraught, his home and belongings gone. Seconds later, further bursts of incendiary rounds crash into the building or bounce off the wall into the street below. Wanton arson on a purely civilian target. As ever, Sarajevo's remarkable firemen fight back, getting their hoses to the flames, for once unhampered by a cut of the water supply. For the fire chief, water is not the main concern. His engines are running out of fuel, and he tells us he won't be able to cope with another fire this day. "The fall of [indiscernible] and escalation of shelling here in the center of Sarajevo again underlining the importance of international efforts in Bosnia. Cease-fires and political talks have lead nowhere and won't until the Western world proves it has a true commitment in ending this war. "Aernout van Lynden, Sky News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first, at one point -- thank you. At one point in that video, we see a red object bounce down and bounce over. Can you just tell us what we were seeing there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's a bullet, but the Yugoslav Army had bullets that caused fires. We don't have those within -- we didn't have those within the Dutch forces, in which I served, and, as far as I'm aware, in NATO countries before, prior to 1989. These are bullets -- incendiary rounds, as they are called, which are there to cause fire in a building, and that's what bounced over the head of my cameraman and myself, because I was standing next to my cameraman when he took the shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you discussed it in your statement, but can you just tell us the situation of what happened with the fire-fighters, what you observed once they entered the building and made their way towards the top?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: When we arrived on the scene, and we were driving from central Sarajevo back to the TV station, so this is the sort of more modern part of Sarajevo, we saw the bullets going into this building, and we saw that there were some fires mostly at the top of the building, a couple in the middle of the building. We stopped to film. All the pictures that you see of the close-ups of the building were taken by my cameraman. The pictures that were taken from the side further off of that building, that same building being hit, were taken by a CNN cameraman. We did an exchange of footage that evening. When the firemen arrived, they set off up the staircase, as you could see in the pictures, to the fires at the top of the building. What we then saw was that more fires -- rounds were fired now at apartments lower in the building, and it seemed to us clear that what the people who were doing the firing intended was to try and cause more fires, therefore catching out those who were at the top of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you stated that it was a civilian target in the story we just watched. If you could just explain that. Did you see any indications there -- any fire coming from that building, or how you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, we were, certainly by that stage of the war, very much aware that whenever there was an incident in Sarajevo, the defence from the Bosnian Serb side would be that it had been a legitimate military target or that the Bosnians had been shooting at themselves. And this is December 1992 we are talking about, and so we were quite quick -- I mean, we did this anyway, wherever we went, Was this building used by elements of the Bosnian Army? We did not only meet this one distraught man who you saw in these pictures who lost his flat, we met other people who were living in the flat, and they all went, Are you mad that we would allow the military to use the building, because we know what the repercussions would be. The moment that fire comes from this building, there would be a great deal of fire returning to it, and they all were adamant that it had not been used militarily. Secondly, we checked with the UN. The UN by that stage was much more organised in Sarajevo, by December 1992, than they had been in the initial days of May and June when I had been there, and while they were not very good at ever stopping anyone shooting at each other, what they were good at was telling where fire was coming from. They assured me that as far as their observers were concerned, no fire had emanated from that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could we give that a number, please? That was 40267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P936. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden. Your Honours, that's all I have at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are minded to tender all the exhibits which were not put to the witness now, all the remaining associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, although, as I say, 40264B, which was on my filing, was a mistake, a typo, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're not tending that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any objections to any one of those associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Those will be admitted, and in due course the Court Deputy will circulate his memo as to the number of the exhibits. Now, Mr. Karadzic, for you to cross-examine the witness, you requested 14 hours for your cross-examination of this witness, although you originally requested for 12 hours. However, the Chamber finds that 14 hours isn't a reasonable number of time for your cross-examination. In any event, we explored the possibility to have an extended sitting tomorrow, but due to the fact that one of the Judges has to sit in another case tomorrow morning, so extended sitting will not be possible. And, instead, on Friday we will explore the possibility to start, for example, at 8.30. So that said, I gather that you will have about seven hours -- approximately seven hours in total. And speaking for myself, that should be an adequate amount of time for your cross-examination, as far as you limit your cross-examination to the relevant questions, refraining from making statements, and without putting unnecessary readings to the witnesses. But it's never meant to encroach upon your right to cross-examination, so we'll try our best to go as far as possible, and then at the end of the day we'll see how much we get on with the evidence. And considering how the cross-examination has been conducted, we'll see whether further time for cross-examination is necessary. In that case, we'll ask the witness to come back again, if necessary. So with that comment, let's start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just make a point from my side, is that I have to return to my home, and I cannot stay the whole of Friday morning. I don't know if this has been made clear, but in that case it was done before I entered your courtroom. I have to, at a certain moment, leave because I am booked on a flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been communicated to the Chamber. My understanding is that you have to leave by 11.00 on Friday, and then we'll try our best to conclude your evidence here. But if necessary, we may ask you to come back again in a convenient time. We'll see. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I'm afraid that that will not be sufficient at all, even if we do what Mr. van Lynden and I agreed upon; namely, that most of my questions are put in such a way that yes-or-no answers can be sufficient. However, I'm afraid that Mr. van Lynden will have to come back again if we cannot sit for longer hours tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. van Lynden, and thank you for having been kind enough to meet up with the Defence before this examination. I believe that this will be of assistance, at least to a certain degree. First of all, I would like to ask you to let us have your notes and journals. Of course, we can redact the private parts. We certainly wouldn't go into any kind of private detail. What is of particular relevance is the fact that this material contains some of the things that were not contained in your reports, and it is quite different from everything that we know with regard to these subjects and that is contained in your journals. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honours, I did not agree with Mr. Karadzic yesterday that we should do yes-and-no answers. Mr. Karadzic said that that's what he would like to do. I heard that, but I did not agree to it. The manner in which he asks questions or wishes to have answers is up to him, but I did not agree to that. He did say it, but I did not agree to it. That's the first thing. Secondly, this Tribunal has never asked for my notes before. I'm not -- I have kept many of my note-books. They are currently not in my direct possession, because our possessions are locked up before -- given our move from Holland to Italy, and therefore I would not have instant access to them, nor do I know for certain that I have all my note-books from the periods relative to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought that we had agreed, because I asked you whether we can shorten things and be as efficacious as possible, and you said, That depends on your questions. So if I put such questions, perhaps we can do it. Let me put a question like that now. Was it your understanding that the Muslim army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was fighting for a united, unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, although I would not call it a Muslim army. As I mentioned earlier, throughout Bosnia, when I encountered the Bosnian Army, there was always also non-Muslims within its ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said today, but let me ask you this: Do you know that it was less than 3 per cent, that Serbs accounted for less than 3 per cent of that army, and that is according to their information?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was never given percentages as to the religious background of the force. What I'm saying is that I encountered, if you will, Serbs and Croats in all the units of the Bosnian Army that I ran into during the various stages of the war while I was in Bosnia. Percentages, I was never given, nor did I ask for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you receive information that in the Serb Army there were Croats and Muslims, and that there were even entire units that consisted of Muslims only; yes or no? We can deal with that on a yes -or-no basis, can't we?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I never encountered one Muslim with any Serb unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ask whether there were any, and could you recognise a Muslim or a Serb just by seeing them? Do they differ to such an extent?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No. As I pointed out earlier in my testimony, they are all Slavs. Yes, we did ask. And could we immediately tell? No, certainly not. But we did ask, and we never -- I never encountered one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you should be well informed because you sent such exhaustive reports, and I wonder how come you did not realise that there were Muslims in the Serb Army, even entire units consisting of Muslims only. But let's leave that aside now. You said that even when you were not in a particular location, you, nevertheless, had your own producer and that he was a source of information for you. Who else were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Back to the point about the Muslims in the Serb Army. If there were Muslims in the Serb Army, it was up to the Serb Army or your office to have shown them and introduced them to us, which you never did, nor do I have any recall of ever being told in Pale, by you or by General Mladic, that there were Muslim units fighting within that army. When I was not in a particular location -- I'm sorry, that is completely unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I asked you where you were, when I asked you how come you knew about some things, you said, Well, my producer was there, and that's how I had that particular information. So you had producers in all the republics, didn't you, and you said that they were your source of information in case you were not there yourself? Is that actually the case? And if so, who else were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I brought producers with me. We had a permanent producer based in Belgrade, and then I had field producers who came with me or with the other crews. I wasn't the only team sent by Sky News into Bosnia. And there were always local producers with these teams. They were a source of information, in the sense that they spoke the language, they could speak to everyone. I could not speak to everyone, as I did not speak Serbo-Croat. Other sources of information would be whoever we happened to run into and have a conversation with, whether it be you, yourself, when we were in Pale, or others that we spoke to when we were in Pale, Mr. -- General Mladic, who did give us a briefing before we actually did the interview. We, at various points of the war, went to the Lukavica Barracks and were given various briefings there by military officers, all of these briefings not in front of the camera, I should add, and it's the same wherever we went. We talked to people, and from those people we took information. We didn't always take that information to be correct, but we talked to people and then we tried to work out whether it was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we agree that -- as you had put it, you said that the Serbs shot themselves in the foot. Now, my interpretation of that is the Serbs had lost the media war, if I can put it that way, and if they waged one at all. Can we agree on the fact that the Serb cause was poorly represented in the Western media? The reasons don't really matter, but do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Can I just make clear to Your Honours that Mr. Karadzic is referring to a comment I made yesterday, when I visited him in prison. I said that in my opinion, by making it so difficult for the Western media to work on the Serb side, and that they had done this in 1991 and again later in Bosnia, that the Serbs had, metaphorically, shot themselves in the foot. I believe that the Serb cause, as you put it, was poorly represented in the Western media because the Serb cause was very poorly put to the Serb media -- to the Western media. The reasons for that lie with the Serbs, not with the Western media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the media are very important, and that they affect the public opinion in their respective countries, and that the public opinion affects the positions taken by governments, or do you think that governments influence the media, or is it mutual?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I think it is complex. I don't think it's as simple to say. Yes, of course the media is important, but the level of the importance of the media from one case to another, from one issue to the other, differs a great deal. And while the media can have great influence on public opinion and then on government, it's also the case that sometimes this doesn't happen, whatever the media may do. And even if public opinion is moved, government doesn't also -- always also move as well. It's a complex issue, and it's not a simple black-and-white one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Muslim side was represented by a public relations firm, Ruder and Finn, in the West?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was never put in touch or never contacted by the public relations firm that you mentioned. In fact, I was never contacted by any public relations firm on behalf of any of the parties to the various conflicts in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did hear of that, that they had a public relations firm representing them, the Muslims in the West, I mean; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have no recall of being told that, but then I wasn't in the West. I was in Bosnia. There were various pressure groups of one nature or other that I was told about specifically in the United States and in London, but that's not where I was working. When I was not in Bosnia, I was at home, and I did not encounter any of these groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did this kind of thing happen, and that's what other journalists told us when they were trying to justify what they did and make excuses for themselves, that editors would significantly change their reports?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: My reports were never changed by any editing in London throughout my time in Yugoslavia. I recall only one shot that was once taken out of a story, which the foreign editor decided to do, which was of blood flowing down an injured person's back, and he felt that this was too graphic and unnecessary. I protested, that he should leave my stories alone, and the shot was put back in again. None of my stories were ever edited. Whether this happened to other journalists, that may be the case, but I can't comment on that. I should point out one other thing here. American television journalists have to send their written part of their stories to their offices in New York or Atlanta beforehand. British television does not do so, does not request that; therefore, the reports were mine and then sent to London and then broadcast, and none of the stories, as far as I'm aware, were changed by editors in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree -- or, rather, does this sound plausible to you, that due to sanctions, we could never engage any pressure groups, or lobbying groups, or public relations agency in the West?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was a pressure group in London. Whether this had to be paid for or whether people were doing this for free, I don't know. I never met them. And does it sound plausible to you that because -- to me that because of sanctions, the Serb government in Belgrade couldn't pay for a public relations firm? No, it does not sound plausible to me. If they had wanted to, they would have found the money. It's not a great deal of money to hire a public relations firm for a government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean money, I didn't mean affordability. I meant fear of sanctions. Not a single agency would agree to represent us because in that way they would be violating the sanctions regimen; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in the UN sanctions and whether a public relations firm in the West would have violated that or not. I simply don't know. It's not something that I looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but that's the way it was. Did we agree that you had said that you did not know which party had switched off water, power, cut food supplies, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: You are referring to the conversation we had yesterday about cutting off power, water, food supplies to the city of Sarajevo. My answer to that was that a city does not grow its own food. The water a city produces does not come out of itself. It has to be brought there, and power usually as well. No. Did I have conclusive personal evidence that this was cut by your government or by someone else? No, I don't. But it is clear that a besieged city is no longer in a position to provide its citizens with its own food and water. That has to come from outside. By besieging the city, your government effectively stopped the people of Sarajevo from having access to the normal food and water supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that my government could have stopped it or that they did stop it? Because if you put it this way, then you're saying that you know that they stopped it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I know for a fact that the UN food supply to Sarajevo was repeatedly stopped, for instance, the supplies that came by air because the plane was shot at. On various of these occasions, we were informed by the UN that that shooting had emanated from Serb lines and that they had then brought the air transport of food to Sarajevo to a halt. I would call that a clear case of your government and your forces stopping food coming to the besieged city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, that's not exactly the way it was. We established here with another witness that there were over 10.000 flights and that not a single one of the incidents related to these planes came from the Serb side, but let's move on. Do you agree that you said that you did not always know who it was that was doing the shooting? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the kind of statement you should refrain from making. Mr. van Lynden, would you like to comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the previous witness and the 10.000 flights, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't here to listen to the previous witness, so I'm not aware of what the previous witness said. So I cannot make any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we agree that you did not always know who it was that was doing the shooting; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Did I -- of course I didn't always know. It was an impossibility to know, if you're driving through a city, who's shooting or where they're shooting at, unless you're being hit, or unless you're filming it, in which you can see who is doing the shooting, where the shooting is emanating from. But did I always know? No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we agree that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had positions to the south of the Holiday Inn and that it's possible that they had sniper shooters in the government building, on the museum, and so on? You had said that was possible, that you knew that they had positions to the south of the Holiday Inn and that it's possible that they had sniper shooters in the government building, and on the Assembly building, and on the museum building.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I said it was possible that they had sniping and army positions south of the Holiday Inn, yes. Did I actually visit these positions? The answer is no. But it is certainly possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you weren't conscious of the existence of the Mujahedin unit in the BH Army. Do you still say that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely. You mentioned yesterday a Mujahedin unit, but I thought one particular corps. I was aware by the end of the war that there were certain what you call Mujahedin units. Did I actually see them? The answer is, no, until the war was actually over. Then I did see one unit. But I did not see any such unit, nor did anyone say that they were a member of such a unit when I spoke to them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You visited the staff, the headquarters of General Juka Prazina, but you said that you weren't sure that he was a general, and you actually said that you don't believe he was a general; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: To visit the staff and headquarters would signal an organised military unit. I visited the staff and headquarters of various armies. That is certainly not what I saw with Juka Prazina. I saw him in a normal civilian apartment, either on the ground floor or in the basement of a building in Sarajevo. Hardly a headquarters, I imagine. I saw him in one or two other buildings later on during 1992 which were, again, of a similar nature. So headquarters, absolutely not. No one ever, in my knowledge, called him "General." They called him, "Juka," and I was not aware that he was given that title, if such be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you, and you said that you didn't know of the existence of other generals who were promoted to that rank from criminals, such as Celo -- there are several people with the same name Celo, and their commander said that there were nine or eleven Celos, but two of them were most prominent, and then Musan Topalovic, Caco, and so on. So is that right, that you weren't aware of that? You weren't informed of that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm aware of -- I'm not aware of 11 Celos. I was aware of one. And I'm aware that there were other people, but I was not ever informed that they had the rank of general, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Two more questions before the break, Your Excellency, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are two things I have to ask you before the break, and then after the break we'll move on to another area. The first thing I want to ask you is this: You said that the BH Army did not have an artillery at that time from June 1992, but roughly when was it did you realise that they did have an artillery in the city of Sarajevo? And, secondly, that you ascribed to me -- or, rather, two things as being my position: first of all, that I said that I consider the Muslims to be Turks, I consider them to be Serbs, and that I wanted to build a wall in Sarajevo. Those are two things that only you seem to know. Nobody else knows about that. And if that is the case, why didn't you publish that, because it's rather drastic and picturesque. If Karadzic was in favour of a wall in Sarajevo, that should surely have been publicised in all the media; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Okay. We are dealing with all sorts of different issues here. The first one is the question of artillery on the Bosnian side within Sarajevo. I have never, during my entire time, seen what I call artillery. I have, in March 1994, seen, at a weapons collection point organised by the UN, 120-millimetre mortars. These are heavy mortars. I would personally not describe that as artillery, but that could be an argument. I never saw the kind of artillery pieces that I saw at the position General Mladic took when I was in Sarajevo. Next question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The wall, and that Muslims were Turks.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we had various conversations late in the evenings in Sarajevo -- in Pale in September 1992. These conversations were off-the-record conversations, as I -- this was not something -- or I didn't have my cameraman there, these were not proper interviews, and I did not use, in my reports, things that you said during those conversations. You -- and I recall this absolutely as one of the options, not the only one, but one of the options, was that you said that a wall should be built in Sarajevo. When asked about this by investigators of this Tribunal, I told them about it. Yesterday, you mentioned something which you called the Brussels solution. I have absolutely no recall of you ever using that description when we spoke in September 1992. The final point is about you saying that they were Turks. That is how I recall it. You said to me yesterday that you consider them Serbs. If you consider them Serbs, it now seems to me, it seems, rather strange that we ever had this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, civil wars happen within the same people. Why not a war? Civil wars are civil wars. Now, do you consider that if it was all right for you not to use informal conversations in your reports, why is it all right if you're using it in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's not a proper question for the witness. This is a court hearing, not a report, and there is -- the witness has explained his answer, why he didn't use them in press reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness is able to answer the question, I'll leave it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour. I was asked to tell the truth about conversations for a court of law. I consider that to be different than when you're reporting for a television station. If I had made those comments known by you, I could not have approved them, because it was not a formal interview and we did not have a camera present there. You could, therefore, have said that it's not true, what I said. Apart from that, my understanding of those conversations was that this was an informal conversation. This is a court of law, and I think that's a different matter, where one is asked to tell the truth, as close as you can get to it. That's why I told the investigators when I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we're going to find that in your notes. I assume you made an entry and recorded it in your notes, because it's so drastic and something that springs to mind that you must have recorded it in your memoirs, if not anywhere else. And just by the by, I drink red wine.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: So do I, but I recall you drinking white wine. That may be a loss of memory on my part. I don't know if it's in my notes, and do not have memoirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, with that, we'll have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. van Lynden, of this story number 5, where you say that the skyscrapers of UNIS, the UNIS skyscrapers, that they were disintegrated and that it was a symbol of the destruction of the town, itself. And then I think you went on to say that the Serbs had signed a truce, but that they did not respect the cease-fire, and that in keeping with that, the Muslims, or the BH Army, as you term it, did not have any artillery, and you said, I think in an attachment, that they stood up to the artillery with small-calibre weapons, infantry weapons. Now, can I ask -- well, I'd like 1D1208 to be called up on e-court, please, and then we can take a look and see what it is you're reporting about to your viewers. We have the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim part, Alija Izetbegovic, and his army commander speaking, or the chief of the Main Staff, rather, Mr. Sefer Halilovic. It's the minutes -- well, actually, we can just have the English version put up on our screens so we can see it better. It was a Presidency meeting, a session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on the 17th of June, 1992, and it's a tape-recording of that. May we have page -- let me just see. Page 3? Page 3 in the Serbian version. It's a short document, and I don't know whether we have that in English. It's page 3 of the English, I assume. [In English] Page 3. [Interpretation] "The Sarajevo situation and the general situation in the Sarajevo area," says Sefer Halilovic - it's him speaking. First of all, the distribution is as follows. In the municipalities, the transversals, you have the Chetnik forces, that is to say, the Serb forces, and they make up -- there are 300 to 400 men. In the Trnovo municipality, there are 300 to 400 men, supported by two tanks to two to three armoured vehicles, mortars, and so on. Now let's see what it says on page 6 of the Serbian version, and I suppose it's the same page of the English. Yes, it says "page 6," so where it says "page 6." "During," it starts "during ," that's right. Now, Sefer Halilovic is reporting to the Presidency about the situation at the battle-front, and it says: "During the two months of battle, the aggressor suffered large casualties, especially losses in material-technical assets, around 20 tanks, 20 transporters, six VBRs, five Howitzers, seven 120-millimetre mortars," et cetera. "Certain number of lost or destroyed assets, three tanks, six armoured vehicles, five Howitzers, 155 millimetres, six mortars, a certain number of infantry weapons, and a large quantity of infantry artillery ammunition seized. Due to a significant loss in assets and artillery rocket assets, the intensity of the artillery actions against Sarajevo decreased." Now, did you report about those Serb losses? Did you report to your viewers? Did you inform them of these Serb losses, your audience, your public?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems to me that I'm being asked a whole bunch of different questions simultaneous, because we began with something quite different and now we come to -- if I understand this correctly, this is from the 17th of June, I have not seen this document before. I'm seeing this document for the first time. The final question is whether we reported this to our -- back to London. Firstly, we -- by the 17th of June, I believe I had left Bosnia. I do not know the precise dates of the events that Mr. Halilovic is referring to in the loss of Serb assets. When we left Sarajevo after the bombardment and some of the stories that we -- that the Prosecution has shown today, we went to Pale and asked you to work there. We -- every single time we left the Pension Olympic, we were arrested. How were we meant to be able to report on Serb losses? Apart from that, it is my experience during the war that all sides were not particularly good at taking journalists along and saying, This is what we've lost. I don't think any government around the world is very good at saying, Here we've made a mistake, and this is what we've lost. I was certainly not taken by the Bosnians to places that they had lost, but I wasn't taken by your forces either. When I reported at the end of the year of 1992 that Zuc had been lost by the Bosnian Serb forces to the Bosnian Army, this is something that was never verified by your government, and, indeed, it led to the anger of General Mladic with me, or it was one of the reasons that he seemed to be angry, when I encountered him in 1994. So, no, we did not -- I mean, I did not at this time -- I don't think I was in Bosnia anymore at that stage. I did not report this, I was not aware of this, we were not made aware by your government of these losses, nor do I actually ever remember being given something of this nature by the Bosnian government, a breakdown of the military achievements that they had made. Would we have reported it? If we had reported it, Mr. Karadzic, we have been told by the Bosnian government that the Serbs have lost all this, you would have said that is completely ridiculous and biased reporting, You haven't checked with us. One of the problems about working in a war zone is that you can't cross lines to verify on an immediate basis, so I would have thought it very unlikely that we would have reported this unless we had had direct confirmation from your government or from your military forces that that was, indeed, the case. Otherwise, it might have been said that we were reporting Bosnian propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a rather lengthy answer, but you see, Mr. van Lynden --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was a rather lengthy question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, you can say yes or no now. What I claim is that your reports were so biased and hadn't been checked out properly that the gentlemen in this hall here, watching your footage and films, gained the impression that it was the Serbs who were doing the shooting, that nobody was actually shooting at the Serbs, and that the city was unarmed, without any artillery, without any soldiers, without any actions going on, and the Serbs without having suffered any losses. Would that be right? Were you biased, were you prejudiced? Did you want to check out the information the Muslims gave you, just as you wanted to check out what the Serbs told you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's a comment, then three, four questions. You would never get a yes-or-no answer to that from any witness. If you want yes-or-no answers or short answers, you're going to have to ask direct, contained, closed questions. The witness can't possibly deal with all those matters, except by giving a very lengthy reply, which he may well now wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether I'm biased or not I leave to the Court to decide for itself. I do not believe I was biased in my reporting. I will say that I have a bias against war, in general, after nearly 25 years of being a war correspondent. Did we check? Yes, we always try to check specifically with the UN. The UN was in Sarajevo in May and June of 1992, albeit not in the kind of numbers as later, but we did try to check with them. We would try to check with both sides as far as possible, but often it was an impossibility. We simply didn't get answers. I think the channel that I worked for gave you, personally, ample opportunity to put your point of view. One of the reasons why I didn't do a sit-down interview with you in Pale in September 1992 is because we had agreed, and Sky News had agreed, that because you speak English, they could interview you directly from London, and many interviews were done with you to make your case. But if we asked for precise information of the kind of nature that you're showing here, a reaction, we wouldn't have got it. We would not have got it on either side, I'd have to say, of the front-lines. Now, let me just read through your question again. No, I don't think I gave an impression that the city was unarmed. We, indeed, filmed soldiers, policemen, as the Court has seen today, firing with small arms. Our general impression at the time, backed by those who we spoke to at the UN, who I would see as unbiased people that we could go and speak to, all said that all the heavy weaponry was basically on your side. I'm not discounting that they did have some heavy mortars. I did, indeed, see heavy mortars, as I've already testified. I did not see, in Sarajevo, heavy artillery. There were definitely soldiers. At the beginning, it was very much ragtag. There was no Bosnia Army when the war began. There were the Territorial Defence forces, there were the police forces, and then units came up, indeed a number of them led by criminal elements, as to which I've testified, Jusuf Prazina being one that I personally knew. You mentioned others. I'm aware that those existed. And I'm also aware that we put those on air and talked about that. So I do not think that that is a case of biased reporting, no. I hope I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree that my questions are rather complex, but that's because I'm under time constraints. If we had sufficient time, things would be different. But let's clarify one thing, Mr. van Lynden. Up until September, were you at Pale up until September or weren't you at Pale by June? I mean Sarajevo, not Pale. Sarajevo. You said a moment ago that in June, at this particular time, that you were no longer in Sarajevo. However, in your reports, it says you were there until September and then that you returned in October. That's on page 11 of the transcript today. Page 11 of the transcript, you said that you were there until September.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I was there until September. I arrived towards the end of May, left at a certain moment in June when -- and came to Pale, because it was the only manner in which we could get our footage out. I then left. I returned to Sarajevo and was there from later in June, throughout July, until the beginning of August, when I left again and went home to my family. I was in London for the London Conference, where we met each other. And then from there, we met each other in Belgrade, and then I spent three to four weeks based in Pale after that. So I was -- and I do not claim to have been in Sarajevo the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the Prosecutor read out that you arrived in Sarajevo in late May 1992 and that you remained there until September. Pale is a municipality of Sarajevo, so when you were at Pale, you were actually at Sarajevo. But let's move on. Can we scroll down the page to see what General Sefer Halilovic says about what they have in Sarajevo. And he says: "The deployment of forces of the Territorial Defence of the Sarajevo region --" Do we have that in English anywhere? It's the last paragraph: "The position and state of the territorial defence forces in Sarajevo ..." We can move on to the next page in English now: "... are composed of the following: The regional staff of the Territorial Defence; two 120-millimetre battery launchers with 12 weapons; 105-millimetre Howitzer battery with five weapons; artillery unit, 122 millimetres, three weapons; an armoured mechanical unit, a group consisting of one tank and five armoured vehicles; 16 Territorial Defence municipal centres; 16 TO companies, around 500 independent units or platoons; around 450 independent groups or companies; and around 100 anti-sabotage units." Now, is it possible that you didn't see that vast armed force in Sarajevo, that it escaped you in some way, Mr. van Lynden? Were you aware of this presence -- military presence in Sarajevo, as described here?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was aware of a large number of men armed with Kalashnikovs, as I've already testified. I was not aware that they had 105-millimetre Howitzer battery. "With five weapons," I'm not quite sure precisely what that means, whether there was one gun or whether there was five. I would not call this -- there was a vast number of men with guns, but this kind of armament is almost insignificant in comparison to the kinds of heavy armament that your forces had at their disposal. But I was not aware of it. No, I didn't see artillery. I've testified I have not see artillery in Sarajevo during my time there, apart from 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A little further down, he said a total of 190-odd thousand, of which 45 per cent were armed. You're right, not everybody was armed. But since the weapons remained up at the front-lines, that was sufficient for those up at the front-line to be armed. So 500 independent platoons, 450 independent companies, and 100 anti-sabotage platoons or units. So that is a vast armed force in Sarajevo. Sarajevo was a fortress, entrenched, full of weapons and soldiers, and you seem to be reporting as if it was a kindergarten or a nursery attacked by the wild Serbs. Well, the Serbs would have too many reasons to be disappointed with reporting of this kind and dissatisfied with it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I can't speak for how the Serbs view my reporting and whether they're dissatisfied or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may we move on to page 7. We have page 7 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said today, and in your report as well, that it was your assessment that those who were killed and wounded were civilians because soldiers wear uniforms, whereas civilians don't, and that that was the criterion that you used when distinguishing between civilians and soldiers. Now, I'd like to focus your attention on the English passage, where it says: "During --" and it's still Sefer Halilovic speaking. He says -- let's see where that is. It's on page 7: "During the initiated attack ..." Yes, the previous sentence. The personnel dressed in civilians [as interpreted]. So the armed people were dressed in civilian clothes, and they had no protection against the elements. And then it says: "Due to -- regardless of the problems, the TO units in the city of Sarajevo were successfully defending the outskirts of the city. They are preventing an attack on the city and simultaneously engaging in actions in selected directions. During the initiated attack, strong Chetnik forces were broken up in the area of Pofalice and Zuc-Mojmilo Brdo, the front stretches below Kromolj towards Orlovac and above Barice and Odzak towards Vasin Han, Ophodzi-Vidikovac, Pljevinac, Osmice - Stari Grad, below the MUP school in Vrace, Mojmilo Brdo and a part of Debelo Brdo. In the last five or six days, the activities of our artillery became especially prominent. They were effective and caused significant losses to enemy soldiers, and material-technical assets in the region of Pofalice, Zuc, Mojmilo Brdo, Vrace, Zlatiste, Osmice, Poljana, and the village of Mrkovici. Based on the current balance of forces, the TO units of the city of Sarajevo can successfully defend the positions they hold, and with certain offensive actions they can even extend the lines of defence." And now my question, Mr. van Lynden: This is a report by the command of the Muslim army to the Muslim Presidency, or whatever you'd like to call it, where he says that the fire that you showed to your audience was -- that the Serb firing was more successful than the Serbs, and that the Serbs suffered losses, and that they were very successful in their artillery attacks. Now, from your reports, can we conclude what Sefer Halilovic is saying here in his report to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly, you would have to ask Mr. Halilovic what he was precisely referring to and what dates these attacks took place on and whether this was if this -- I doubt that this was the same as what I was reporting on, because that was not action happening along the front-lines. This was shelling coming in throughout the city. He reports attacks on the front-lines. I haven't seen this document before. I don't know if Mr. Halilovic, indeed, wrote all this down. But, firstly, let's take the question right at the beginning about the military being in uniform or not being in uniform. In a report that has not been shown to the Tribunal, but made also in the early days of June, I state quite clearly that there is a mish-mash within the Bosnian armed forces. Some of them are in uniform, many of them are not. They were not all in uniform at that stage of the war, and we made that clear. When we encountered wounded people, and in the one report that was shown to this Court this afternoon, after heavy shelling and there was fighting, we made clear that the wounded men were armed members of the Bosnian Army who had been launching a counter-offensive. We didn't say that these were civilians. We said these were members of the armed forces. Of course, with any man in a war zone who is under the age of, let's say, 60, and he's dressed in civilian clothes, you can say, Well, he was an army, and if somebody else says he was a civilian, what do we say? On the whole, I think we made it clear who the civilians were, and it was clear to us, and who the armed forces were, and we made that, I think, clear in the reports that this Tribunal has seen today. As far as the attacks are concerned, as I understand the reading of what Mr. Halilovic reported to his president, was that these were armed actions undertaken by the Bosnian forces along the front-lines. That's on the edge. He doesn't mention fighting in the center of the city, at Grbavica here. And the shelling that we showed and filmed on those days in early June was shelling that landed throughout Sarajevo. There's a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just clarify this. This is a session of the Presidency held on the 17th of June. Halilovic is reporting about the previous period, the previous two or three weeks. He is reporting about the very same events that your report pertained to. However, in the middle of this paragraph - please take a look - he is mentioning the old city, Osmice, Ophodzi, Vasin Han. He is mentioning the parts of town that are in their hands and from which they are operating. Of course, you know that Stari Grad or, rather, the center of the city is Velesici; right? Do you see where he says "Stari Grad," the old city?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I know that "Stari Grad" means "Old City." Yes, I see. I don't see him saying that there were attacks from the Stari Grad towards your lines. As I see it, he is saying here that an initiated attack -- strong Chetnik forces were broken up in the area of Pofalice, Zuc, and Mojmilo Brdo. That's not the center of Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go on. Look at the very same sentence, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to try to be clear, I'm looking at the translation provided by the Defence, if we are talking about page 7, the report is about "the past five to six days," not "the past two to three weeks," if -- so I think that was either a misstatement, or a translation problem, or a different section of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate me to the part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the middle of what in the English says is page 7, which is on page -- it's marked as page 7 in the translation, on page 2 of the English in e-court, in the third paragraph down which begins: "Despite the aforementioned problems ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And "the last five or six days," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is that section I thought Mr. Karadzic was directing the witness to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, if we look at page 6, this pertains to operations over two months. For example, on page 6, the first paragraph, it says: "During the two months of operations, the aggressor suffered" such and such casualties. Well, they were not self-inflicted; right? It is an account of action taken by them, so they are bragging about all the losses that they caused on our side. And you will see that this is a second session on the 17th, so he's talking about the preceding period. And there were some special operations perhaps over the past five or six days. However, that is the entire reporting period. And it says here where the front-line is, and, of course, it is the front-line that is being operated from and operated against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Whom are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your question? Let's move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is page 138 in Serbian. However, let's have a look now. This was 7, wasn't it, now 8, 9, 10 -- page 11, page 11 in Serbian. And we have it here, 11, page 11. It says here: "In the next stage, 10 to 15 days, the Territorial Defence of the RBiH shall carry out the following activities," and then they are listed. And what it says about Sarajevo: "In the region of Sarajevo, the city of Sarajevo will be defended by active operations within the city, and deblockade should be carried out along the axis Nova Gradiska-Ilidza-Blazuj-Kiseljak-Centar-Vogosca- Ilijas-Visoko, and in the Gorazde region the road to the Drina River valley should be deblocked."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about what was being planned and that it is primarily offensive operations that are being planned around town and from town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, if he can break up the questions a bit, it will be easier for the witness to answer. It's: "Did you get this information?" There's about three questions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Make your questions simple, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. van Lynden, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic question seems to be in reference to the line of that there would be active operations by the Bosnian Army - this is the Bosnian command, I'm told, to his president - within the city and at other areas. Did I get that information? No. Would it be likely that any army gives the information prior to launching an attack to a foreign journalists? The answer is no. The operation that we were aware of, while it was happening in Sarajevo, and they admitted it was their operation, this was an attack which we couldn't go to the outskirts to film, but we filmed the men who came back from that operation wounded to the hospital. We reported that that was a Bosnian operation. That, we knew about, and that was admitted to us. I'm aware that -- let me put it this way: Military commanders will say a lot of -- make a lot of statements to their political leaders. I'm also aware that it doesn't always work out. There were many operations launched throughout the war in Bosnia by the Bosnian forces to try and break through the siege of Sarajevo. As far as I'm aware, those operations did not succeed. I'm not aware of any operation being announced to a Western journalist beforehand, and even at certain moments, for instance, in the summer of 1995, there was a refusal of the Bosnian Army to even confirm that such an operation was underway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P934, could I have that briefly, please. It's a map, a Prosecution map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you -- I'm sure that you know this much. While we're waiting for that, actually, it's a bit easier for me now if you were not impartial, if you were simply uninformed. The outcome is the same, but I find it easier to take this way. Now, Mr. van Lynden, can you mark, for instance, who is around this Serb zone? You see this Serb zone where you put that arrow? And then on the north and on the west, who is there around us? It says "HVO"; right? And if you could mark --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mark what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, mark who is where. The blue line is the Muslim line, right, the Muslim Croat line; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the red one right next to it is the Serb line. I see. And then the area beyond that, are those Muslim government forces to the left and to the north of the blue line, and down there to the south of the blue line, beyond the blue line?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That would be territory controlled by the Bosnian Army or by the HVO, yes. And the other territory would be controlled by your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is within the red lines is controlled by the Serb forces, and what is beyond the blue lines is under the control of the Muslim Croat forces; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that when Halilovic speaks about offensive activities coming from the outside and from within, that what he actually means is that the de-blockade of Sarajevo should take place through attacks from Central Bosnia and from the city of Sarajevo itself; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware, at least, that in the summer of 1995 that was tried and that it failed. And obviously it was tried and failed during other periods of the war. The siege, as I said earlier, was never broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you identify Ilijas on this map? Do you know where Ilijas is here? Down the road -- down the river to the north, actually; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Ilidza would be in the area, let's see, around here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That would be Rajlovac, rather. No, Rajlovac. Nedzarici, Rajlovac, but Ilijas is to the north.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: If you say so. I'm not aware of being in Ilijas, apart from possibly in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. van Lynden, Ilijas is the location where most of the shells in this war fell, and proportionately their losses were the great -- civilians and soldiers, Sarajevo municipality that totally -- that your interest did not focus on at all?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, if that's the case, why were we not taken there by your government and by your army? If we are not shown and we are not told, how are we meant to know? You cannot have correspondents in a war zone running around freely without -- to front-lines. If you didn't show us, how is the rest of the world to know? I was never taken there by your government or by your army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It was published all over, but never mind. Thank you. I just wanted the Trial Chamber to see that we are all surrounded. They are surrounding us, and we are surrounding them; semi-encirclement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have the opportunity to make your submission. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's the question: Are we semi-encircled by them, like they are semi-encircled by us?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The city of Sarajevo wasn't semi-encircled. It was completely encircled and besieged. The distances of what you call your encirclement at certain points is tight, absolutely, but on the whole it is not. And the two are incomparable, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, an UNPROFOR military officer said that it was an encirclement, not a siege, not a blockade, but we'll get to that. Thank you for the map. Now I would like to move on to this document again, page 12, I think, I think. If the previous one was 11, then this would be 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, I haven't been objecting really hardly at all today, but this is the kind of comment, that an UNPROFOR officer said this or that and we'll get to it later, wastes time and isn't a question. And most times Mr. Karadzic doesn't come back to these points and is simply making argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. So can we pull up the 1D1208 again. So, Mr. Karadzic, did you understand what Mr. Nicholls has said right now? You should refrain from making such statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nicholls knows who I'm talking about. They have that material. Can I have page 12 now. Now we have page 12. Mr. Izetbegovic is asking the following: "When adding up the engagement of enemy manpower near Sarajevo that is holding town in encirclement," so, see, Izetbegovic also says "encirclement," "how much is that?" And Halilovic says: "About 6.000 in Sarajevo, or, rather, those who are holding Sarajevo encircled. As for manpower, in our estimate, which I believe is realistic, it's about 80.000 in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So Halilovic estimates that the Army of Republika Srpska has 80.000 soldiers throughout Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is page 13, then. Page 13. Sorry about that. Yes, we have it now. This is Halilovic's response: "There are around 6.000 in the city of Sarajevo," I mean Serbs, and he probably didn't take into consideration those in Central Bosnia, and he says that in Bosnia-Herzegovina there are about 80.000 Serb troops: "However, for the city of Sarajevo to be completely conquered, much stronger forces are required than what they have," I mean "they," the enemy. "Objectively, that cannot -- they cannot accomplish that in the near future unless some radical turning points occur. However, they will still attempt to accomplish this goal, and the goal is to divide the city of Sarajevo and merge the parts from Rajlovac over Stup and Lukavica with Pale. For that goal, objectively they need to have certain forces at their disposal, but in that case their defence would weaken in other areas; hence, even now it is unrealistic that they are able to do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. van Lynden, this is his own estimate of his own forces of Sarajevo; 500 independent battalions, 450 independent companies, and here there are 6.000 Serbs and 80.000 Serbs in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you know about this vast disproportion in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Firstly, back to the line as to how many battalions and independent units Mr. Halilovic had within -- at his disposal within Sarajevo, I came out of an alley where a battalion was usually around 700 men. I've encountered battalions in other countries where it's suddenly only about 100 men. I see no actual figures that Mr. Halilovic gives as to the precise number of men in companies or battalions, so I am unclear as to the entire -- the number of men at his disposal in Sarajevo. As far as your larger question is concerned, that, as you say, there were only 80.000 Serb troops within Bosnia-Herzegovina, it did become clear in September 1992 that, in terms of personnel, you were probably out-numbered by the Bosnian forces. In terms of weaponry, there was no comparison between the two. You completely out-gunned them in every single way in the form of artillery, tanks, armoured personnel carriers. They simply did not have that kind of weaponry, so the one made up for the other. There was a problem of manpower on the Serb side, but you did have 80.000 fully you armed men backed by heavy arms, and that kind of backing was not there on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He actually said that on that earlier page, page 7, that he had 91.000 men, 500 independent platoons, 450 companies, and so on and so forth, but that doesn't matter now. What does matter, Mr. van Lynden, is that we agree that against us -- well, if there were one and a half million of us, there were 3 million against us. So the ratio was 2.1 in favour of the Muslim Croat Federation, as far as mobilisation was concerned; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In terms of manpower, to a degree, but there was a split between the Bosnian forces and those of the Croats. And then, as I said before, you can call up men, but if they don't have a gun, they're not much good to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now you are making me show information provided by the Secretary-General of the UN, you are tempting me to do that, where he says that a shortage of weapons is no longer an issue, as far as the Bosnian Serb side is concerned. However, we've already shown that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this previous document, the transcript from the session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 17th of June, be admitted, and could I have in e-court 1D01130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. I just notice that on some pages it appears that only one sentence is translated. I don't object to the document, but we hope for a fuller translation at some point so we can read around this one sentence of page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification, pending translation. And the exhibit number will be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D192, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that what was used by the Defence and what can be translated can be admitted. I mean, we had this translated privately, and who needs a translation can have it translated. So could I now please have 1D01130 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, you read out some part from page 3, but only one line was translated. Without full translation, we have difficulty in understanding those parts. So we marked it for identification, pending full translation of those parts. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Unfortunately, there is no translation for this yet. However, I am going to read the document out. It is The service of National Security of Republika Srpska. The date is the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, this is about localities that you presented in your reports. And now I'm going to read this to you. It's entitled, "Information," and then it says: "In the former barracks of Marsal Tito and at the Faculty of Civil Engineers and the Faculty of Architecture, training is taking place of members of the so-called TO BiH. According to the same information, in these barracks there is a centre for the training of members of the so-called TO BiH for rapid interventions, and the training takes about 25 days. In the town of Velesici, there is a tank, and in front of the building of the so-called TO BiH at Ciglane, an APC and a tank are stationed." So, tell me, did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
