utterances.text: What, about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. About the deployment of those forces. Did you know about that? Because you said that the Marsal Tito Barracks were alight, on fire, and it almost brings tears to your eyes, but here we see that it's a legitimate target. Did you know that it was, in fact, a legitimate target with military structures there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't say it was not a legitimate target immediately after its evacuation by the troops of the Yugoslav Army. As far as I'm aware, no one used it, because this document says that people are being -- it is being used to train forces. It was certainly not used to train anyone in that period. No one went into it in that period. We, indeed, showed right at the beginning people running out of it. I am aware that Bosnians, I imagine, army units went in to see what they could find immediately following the evacuation of Yugoslav Army troops. That it was later used by the Bosnian Army, but that is afterwards, after the shelling I reported on, is an absolute possibility. I didn't enter it after that period. On one occasion in July, an incident that the Prosecution has asked me about earlier this afternoon, when we saw three people that had been hit on the road, we saw fire emanating from what remained of the Marsal Tito Barracks, a form of covering fire. So there was certainly soldiers in there in July 1992. But in the period that we have seen the various stories that have been shown in court this afternoon, during that period there were no Bosnian Army units within the Marsal Tito Barracks. It would have been very foolish to be there when they come under such sustained fire, let alone that it was used for training at that stage. Afterwards, quite possibly, but during -- when we made those reports, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this tank in Velesici, you can't tell us anything about that, right, because you didn't see it, and you weren't aware of the fact that they had tanks at all; is that right, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I have never seen a tank inside the part of Sarajevo controlled by the Bosnian forces, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "The Main Staff of the so-called TO BiH for this area is located on the premises of the Transport and Technical School, whereas the so-called police station is in the Velesici local commune." Now, let me ask you whether you know where the bus stop in Sarajevo was, the main bus station.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The main bus station that I'm aware of is in the newer part of Sarajevo towards the west. There was another bus station that I'm vaguely aware of. Hard to put its location. In the photograph that I was shown right at the beginning I could -- saw that. But there was certainly a main tram stop. That was to the west, and I imagine there were buses there as well. But in the period when I was in Sarajevo, there were no buses or trams running. It was not something that I looked into as to what was happening with the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Might I be of assistance? Let me remind you. Was the bus station between the Marsal Tito Barracks and the railway station? So right up along the Marsal Tito Barracks wall, then you have the bus stop and the railway station? Do you remember that? If not, we'll come to that tomorrow and we'll indicate it on the map. But let's move on with this document, and for that may I have the next page displayed, please. It says: "The artillery weapons were located on Hum Hill, underneath the relay station of RTV BH and in the Velesici and Kosevsko Brdo. We'd like to mention that tank movement was noticed around the bus station from where they fired, and after that they withdrew immediately." So what I want to say, Mr. van Lynden, is this: That Hum and below Hum, Velesici, and somebody says that Mladic mentioned that here, Kosevsko Brdo, the tunnel, and the bus station from time to time were legitimate targets; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Am I meant to say yes or no, whether they were legitimate targets? If I didn't see military forces there, how can I judge whether they were legitimate targets, Mr. Karadzic? I did not see those tanks there, and therefore I cannot say whether they were or were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's assume they were there. And if they were, would that be a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I've been told never to make assumptions in journalism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The same applies in the law, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Glad to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Would you, as a general principle, if there's military operations and if there are tanks and artillery in a location, from your extensive experience as a war correspondent, would you genuinely take that as being a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, with one qualification. Under the Laws of War, fighting in a city forces the armies concerned to be extremely careful so that you don't cause civilian casualties, and that should be -- it's a part of the Geneva Conventions, as I'm sure that you are more than aware than I, and therefore that should always be a consideration for the military involved. But, yes, of course, generally speaking, in a more general sense, they would be legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in the document there is a enumeration of all the places and localities where there are legitimate targets, so once we have that translated, we'll be able to come back to that. But now let's go to page 3, and I'd like to draw your attention to the UNIS building. It says in the UNIS building is the Territorial Defence of Novo Sarajevo. In the UNIS building, in Masic Street, is the headquarters of the so-called Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina for Novo Sarajevo. We have information according to which the park by Miljetska between the Vranica skyscraper, to the right is a mortar set up on a truck. The staff of the so-called Territorial Defence of BiH for that area, Cengic, Vila, and so on, is located in the Treska [phoen] Furniture Store. At Pero Kosoric Square is a large concentration of troops, more than 1.000 men, and so on and so forth. Now my question: In one of your reports, you said that flats and business premises were turned into places from which they shot. We have that somewhere, I believe, that they were turned into places from which there was shooting; rifles, sniper fire, and the like. Now, here we see a report from the secret police which confirms the fact that these business premises, commercial buildings, UNIS, Treska, Vraniska [phoen], and so on, were, indeed, used for military purposes. So if that was so, were they, too, legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The report you allude to was when we were on one of the front-lines. If your -- if there are a war in an urban battleground, by definition what used to be people's offices or people's houses on the front-line gets turned into military strong points. That's what happens in an urban battleground. Whether, as you say, the UNIS towers was used, I don't know. I didn't see so. I was taken to various territorial defence -- this is not an army. This is territorial defence. We have to remember just what this is. It's something quite different. I saw a number of their headquarters in Sarajevo. I did not see one at the UNIS. Later in the war, I did visit a number of different offices that had been used, and these had been commercial offices, I imagine, that were used as bases -- offices of various units of the Bosnian Army. Where else were they meant to go? They were bound to go to one building or another. Those buildings had previously been of civilian use and were now being put to military use. UNIS towers, I wasn't aware. And we had visited it, and we did not meet anyone during that visit of the Territorial Defence forces there. Therefore, I didn't see it as a logical target. Can I be completely certain, Mr. Karadzic? No. Is everything told to me from the Bosnian side? No. So there is a possibility. But as I said, we did visit the building prior to the attack that was carried out on it. The other points -- the other areas, I can't comment on. I didn't visit every area, and so I just simply -- I don't know. We also, of course, don't know whether this document is actually accurate. We have absolutely no way, or that I can tell, that this document is accurate. That it comes from the secret services, I've seen documents from secret services before that were fairly inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. No objections, Your Honour. I might be wrong, but if the document we're talking about -- I think we begin at page 94, line 15, the date read out is "19th of June, 1992." I'm not sure if it's a typo. I think the document is dated 20th of July, looking at it. So that would need to be corrected if that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, correct, it's dated 20th of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be MFI'd? It's the 20th of July. That's what it says on the first page. And, Mr. van Lynden, just to inform you - this isn't a question - this document was seized by the OTP investigators. They're the ones that got hold of it, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't let that pass. I mean, the witness's comment was about the source of the document, not who seized it ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I was about to ask the position taken by the OTP, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. Tieger, about this document. He seems to be tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. As I think you said, it could be marked for identification and we'll look for the translation, but no objection to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit D193, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now may I have 1D361 displayed, please, 1D361.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Mr. van Lynden, let me just tell you that this a document from the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim part, of course -- the Muslim Croatian part, and in English -- it's in English, and it says on the 14th of June, 1992, Hasan Efendic, a very well-known commander of the Territorial Defence, is re-affirming -- re-asserting a cease-fire. It's the re-affirmation of the cease-fire established on the 1st of June, 1992. So on the 1st of June, 1992, the parties signed a cease-fire agreement. From the 1st of June to the 15th of June, 1992, we see all the offensive actions undertaken by the BH Army and the terrible material and human losses it inflicted on the Army of Republika Srpska. On the 14th of June, he once again expresses his attachment of the cease-fire that was not respected. So did you know that there was a cease-fire in force when you arrived, on that first day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I arrived at the end of May, and I wasn't aware of a cease-fire being in place then. We were told that a cease-fire had been agreed to, and we were told by people at the UN that this was almost instantly broken. When we asked them who had broken it, they said, We cannot initially tell. But we spoke, for instance, to the Australian colonel who is in one of my stories from those days, who was negotiating on behalf of the UN, and he told me that a cease-fire had been broken repeatedly, and obviously it was broken repeatedly, but he blamed the Bosnian Serbs. Secondly, you say that during that time, you -- your people suffered such terrible consequences of the fighting. I was not on your side of the front-lines. I was inside Sarajevo. All I can say is what I witnessed and what we filmed was a form of carnage going on inside the Bosnian-held part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But we heard from Sefer Halilovic, the commander of the Muslim army, about all the losses we suffered and that they were all offensive operations launched by his army. I'd like to tender this document into evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, objection to that argument without any question attached, even a pretence of a question at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are having a habit of making a comment at the end of each question and answer. Please refrain from making such statement. I take it there's no objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D194. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I apologise. But my question was whether we've just read that the commander of the Muslim army informed us about the Serb losses; yes or no. And we looked at the document a moment ago. The 17th of June is the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I have 1D01231 next, please. 1D01231 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm seeing the clock. We'll rise today, and we'll resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of May, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
